tasks.what: Measure prop collisions on the oriented collider, as the game does
tasks.note: Not an exemption in the end -- the check was measuring the wrong shape, and fixing that found three real bugs underneath. (1) It tested the AXIS-ALIGNED box while the game tests the oriented collider, so every fenced build printed FAIL for scenery standing on the board perfectly well. (2) `build.rotated_footprint` only swaps the axes on QUARTER turns, so a prop at 15 degrees was measured at its unrotated extent -- and Scatter used the same function, so the scatter itself was letting through props that really did interpenetrate. (3) A fresh `Scatter` started BLIND: yard fences are laid by _lay_yards before _dress_districts builds its own scatter, so ferns, crates and stumps grew straight through fences already standing. (4) `_dress_yards` was handed a scatter and then placed with `b.prop` anyway, which does no collision test at all -- beds and crates dropped through the yard's own fence. One implementation of the geometry now (build.oriented_box / oriented_aabb / oriented_depth) used by both the scatter that prevents overlaps and the check that reports them. A boundary corner join -- two panels meeting at a penetration no deeper than a panel's own thickness, measured at exactly 0.180 on `Wooden Fence` -- is not counted, because that is how a fence turns a corner and the corners on the board are complete. Result: Pelvesthollow 22%% -> 4%%, Graybank 21%% -> 4%%, East Tradebourne 16%% -> 3%%.

tasks.what: Check no cell holds two ground tiles
tasks.note: BUILT as verify._ground_sheet, and it found a real defect the moment it ran: **every yard on every board built so far was z-fighting.** _lay_yards surfaced its cells after _lay_terrain had already sheeted them in grass -- 365 cells on Pelvesthollow holding `Grass 1x1` + `Swamp floor 1x1`, coplanar. TaleSpire does not drop a co-located tile the way it drops a colliding prop; it keeps both and they dither as the camera moves. **Clearing the cell first is NOT the fix** and was tried: open country is sheeted in 2x2 grass blocks, so taking one up because a single corner of it is a yard strips the ground from three cells that are not -- which is what left ferns standing over nothing. The terrain pass owns the ground sheet now: `surface_role` decides the yard's material with everything else, the 2x2 pass requires four cells to agree on the ROLE and not just the class, and _lay_yards only fences. Knock-on: Pelvesthollow tile seams 5,398 -> 662 and Graybank 21,202 -> 2,302, because the doubled tiles were counted there too; assets down 770 and 2,921.

tasks.note: DONE. tasks.what: Re-size the chunk budget for the denser build, and fix the default
tasks.note: DONE as build.asset_budget, and it is a size-derived budget rather than the flat lower default the task first asked for -- because a flat number is wrong in both directions, measured. **Reducing --chunk-tiles is the wrong lever and makes it worse**: at 96 tiles East Tradebourne FAILS at 31,739 bytes, because a smaller cell leaves more trimmed open-country chunks for _absorb_open_country to fuse back into the kept ones. The budget is what the quadtree splits on. Measured on the rebuilt towns (112- and 80-tile cells): at 9000, Tradebourne 102 chunks / 99.4% of cap; 6500 -> 114 / 79%; 6000 -> 135 / 70%; 5500 -> 159 / 67%. A paste is ~40 s of driving, so 159 against 114 is half an hour. And 6000 pushed *Graybank* from 22 chunks to 37 for headroom a village does not need. tasks.what: Prune the probe and rebuild boards, and record which are worth keeping
tasks.note:
DONE as boards.prunable / boards.unclaimed / boards.keepers and `citysmith boards prune`. Read off the real campaign list (tools/ts.ps1 boards, scrolled both ways): **28 boards, 22 of them 'Unknown Realm N'** -- every one a probe or a town rebuild nobody came back to -- plus two superseded scene names, against 2 tracked scene boards and 4 named by hand. **The first version offered to delete the finished towns.** The registry only ever tracked SCENE boards, so East Tradebourne, Graybank and Pelvesthollow are claimed by nothing, and a rule of 'prune what the registry does not own' listed all three. It now flags only what is provably disposable -- superseded names, and boards nobody ever named -- and reports hand-named strays through `unclaimed` with no recommendation. Deletion stays manual and is NOT driven: Delete board sits behind the per-board triangle immediately beside the play arrow, the rows re-sort on every rename, and there is no undo.

**CORRECTED 2026-08-26, and the correction is the interesting half.** The rule above -- 'boards nobody ever named are provably disposable' -- was itself wrong, in the same direction and for the same reason as the bug it replaced. Driving the live campaign, the board in front of us was `Unknown Realm 22`, holding the newest build of a town its owner wanted, and `prunable` listed it for deletion. **A default name is the absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.** `boards.unnamed` is now a fourth bucket -- reported as LOOK FIRST, never as disposable -- and `prunable` keeps only supersessions the registry itself recorded, which is the one thing here that is actually provable. Note the shape: both versions of this bug inferred 'unwanted' from 'unlabelled', and the campaign list gives a name and nothing else, so no rule keyed on the name can ever do better. The mitigation is upstream -- rename a board when a paste lands, prefix throwaways with `Probe - ` -- not a cleverer heuristic.

tasks.what: Lift the build orchestration out of cmd_build so a UI and the CLI share one path
tasks.note:
BUILT as citysmith/pipeline.py -- build_town() plus BuildResult, with write_chunks and write_multislab moved across too, since they are side effects and leaving them in cli.py would have made pipeline import cli. cmd_build went 138 -> 71 lines, and what is left is crop parsing, palette resolution, a formatter for the progress lines, and five prints. No decisions, no side effects. The README/CLAUDE.md claim that cli.py is a thin shell over the core is now true rather than aspirational.

**Byte-identity was verified against main's own source, not asserted.** A `git archive` snapshot of main run against the same layout into the same out-dir, diffed: four invocations (default; --by-region --multi-slab; --per-building --no-npcs; the whole uncropped town at --seed 33) are identical on stdout, and all 8 written artifacts of the multi-slab case -- four region slabs, the plugin document, paste order, the npc manifest and city-raster.svg -- are identical too. Determinism was established first by running main against itself twice, so the comparison means something.

**The golden test is hermetic on purpose.** A checked-in expected-output string built from the real catalog would carry asset names from whichever TaleSpire packs THIS machine owns -- the same objection that keeps docs/asset-index.md out of the repo -- and would fail on a colleague's checkout. tests/test_pipeline.py drives a permissive stub palette instead, pinning the formatting and orchestration that a refactor actually breaks; the real-catalog diff stays a by-hand check. Stable across PYTHONHASHSEED 1, 7 and 12345.

**progress(stage, **fields) is an API, not a CLI-preservation hack.** Four documented stages in pipeline.STAGES carrying objects and numbers, never sentences, so cli.py renders the four lines it has always streamed and ui-build-screen can render the same events as JSON -- one interface for both callers instead of two that drift. Without it the refactor would have been byte-identical and still a regression: on a 400k-asset East Tradebourne those four lines are the only sign of life for minutes.

One deliberate deviation: the palette resolves BEFORE the rasterise now, so a style the installed packs cannot supply fails before spending seconds rasterising -- at the cost of the tilemap summary no longer printing ahead of that error. Commented at the call site. Two pre-existing oddities found and preserved rather than fixed: --multi-slab writes its document and prints nothing, and MULTISLAB_HELP -- which explains how to paste the thing -- is defined and referenced nowhere. The path is on the result as `multislab` now, so wiring the help in is two lines.

tasks.what: A stdlib HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 serving the sidecar, with a typed JSON API
tasks.note:
BUILT as citysmith/uiserver.py plus citysmith/ui/{index.html,app.css,app.js} -- stdlib http.server, hand-written page, no bundler, no CDN, one package-data stanza so the page ships with an installed citysmith. All four safety clauses are enforced and each has a test; I probed every one over live HTTP rather than reading the tests.

**Loopback**: make_server RAISES for any host not in LOOPBACK -- verified 0.0.0.0, ::, a LAN address and a hostname all refused, 127.0.0.1 bound. There is no flag or env var that changes it. A DNS-rebinding guard rejects any request whose Host header is not loopback (Host: evil.com -> 403), no Access-Control-* header is ever sent, and CSP is default-src 'self'.
**Named operations**: no endpoint takes a command string. Verified live -- style 'medieval; rm -rf /', seed '$(whoami)', roofs '1; echo hi', fence_style 'posts', hour 'dusk', chunk_tiles 999999 and stem '../../evil' are all 400 with a message naming the legal values, and an unknown key is a 400 rather than being ignored. **seed: true is rejected** -- bool is an int subclass, so a checkbox would otherwise pass as 1. The source is an id from the server's own scan, never a path.
**Paths**: resolve_in rejects `..` by name, absolute paths and symlink escapes by comparing resolved paths, then an extension allowlist. Five live escapes refused including %2f, %2e%2e%5c and the `....//` collapse trick.
**The key** stays server-side: /api/options reports only ai_available as a bool, connect-src 'self' stops the page reaching api.anthropic.com, and a test plants a sentinel ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and asserts it appears in no response body.

Polling rather than SSE, because a poll leaves no half-open connection when the page is closed. POST /api/build returns 202 with a job id AND NOTHING ELSE, so no caller can be written that blocks on the report. A second concurrent build is a 409 -- write_chunks deletes the stem's previous output, so two builds in one directory produce half of each.

tasks.what: Drive import and build from the UI, and show the verify report and raster
tasks.note:
BUILT. Findings render one row each with the level chip and **the whole detail sentence**, pre-wrap so indented continuation lines keep their indent -- no clamp, no ellipsis, no 'show more'. Order is Report.text()'s, worst first, pinned by a test against a deliberately unsorted input. A one-line verdict sits above (BUILT CLEAN / WITH WARNINGS / FAILED, plus the fail/warn/pass counts) so there is something to read at a glance WITHOUT reducing the findings to a tick; filter chips hide rows by level and never reorder or shorten.

**The chunk list is numbered by walking result.paste_order and looking each file up, so the on-screen order IS paste order by construction** rather than by a sort that could be changed. A test checks it against <stem>-paste-order.txt on disk. Layer headings, tile spans, asset and byte counts, building counts, a #/. grid map, per-file downloads, and the CLI's own PASTE_HELP / TILE_HELP imported from cli.py rather than duplicated. city-raster.svg below with a zoom slider.

One column by default, two only above 1040 px, no fixed widths, light and dark both defined -- the target is a second monitor, where a tall narrow column is as likely as a wide one.

**Known and deliberate**: with all filters on, the pass block is a wall of full sentences -- Forest Church returns 17 findings, several over 200 characters. That is the trade the brief asks for (those sentences cost a dozen sessions) and the filter chip is the release valve. Settled on screen under ui-onscreen.

**The "import" half of that sentence was only half true until 2026-08-29, and this note said otherwise for every session in between.** `run_build` called `importers.import_layout(source.path, seed=...)` and passed no options at all, and `_FIELDS` -- the request allowlist -- carried none of them, so every knob `citysmith import` offers was reachable from the command line and from nowhere on the page: --whole-canvas, --margin-ft, --house-ft, --cluster-gap-ft, --no-fences, --no-clip, --name. Measured on samples/sedgewater.geojson: the default import is 21 buildings on 138x114 tiles, and core_only=False with margin_feet=200 is 24 buildings on 227x203. A UI user silently lost three outlying farms and had no control on the page to prevent it, while a CLI user typed one flag. The screen drove *build*, and only build.

Now: seven fields on an Import fieldset, typed by the same rules as the rest of the form -- `_float` bounded and finite, `_town_name` patterned like `_STEM`, an unknown key still a 400, and `import_layout` called with its keywords spelled out one by one exactly as `build_town` is (test_import_layout_is_called_with_spelled_out_keywords, which also asserts every offered field reaches the call -- this bug's own shape). The fieldset shows only for a GeoJSON source and `formBody` drops the fields to match, because a layout.json is already imported and every control there would be inert on one.

**Two things the wiring forced, and each is the same defect in a smaller way.** `json.loads` accepts the bare literals Infinity and NaN, which pass a range check on one side and fail it on the other with a message about nothing -- an infinite margin is a board with no size -- so `_float` tests finiteness first and names it. And an option the reader drops has to be SAID: `importers.options_for` is the public lookup for which format takes which option (MFCG exports geometry only, so it has no settled core to crop to and no fences to drop), `unused_import_options` reports only what somebody actually changed, and the job log carries a NOT USED line. That is `verify.feature_report`'s rule applied to a request instead of to a map: an option that is set, dropped and never mentioned looks exactly like one that was honoured -- which is precisely how this shipped and stayed shipped.

Driven on the running page as well as in the suite: sedgewater imports at 227x203 with 24 buildings through the form; a layout source reports all three chosen options as NOT USED; an MFCG export reports cluster_gap_ft, core_only and fences while honouring margin_feet. The evidence field takes one symbol, so it still points at the report half -- the import half is pinned by test_the_import_options_reach_the_importer.

tasks.what: Drive the paste from the UI, and say plainly when it cannot
tasks.note:
BUILT as citysmith/pastedrive.py (the subprocess half) plus the paste screen and endpoints in uiserver. **The split is the same one chatsession made, for the same reason**: uiserver.py still contains no subprocess -- the only match is the docstring stating the guarantee -- so test_nothing_in_the_server_can_reach_a_shell survives untouched instead of being deleted to make room. pastedrive has its own guard asserting on the CAPTURED ARGV that -Recipe/-Name/-Stem/-OutDir/-ShotEvery are separate list entries, so 'no composed shell string' is checked against what is actually spawned rather than against the source text.

**An unreadable probe is not a pass, and that is the whole point of the task.** read_plane_state recognises the literal prefix 'build plane off' and returns off | on | unknown | unreadable; only `off` proceeds. Verified independently against the three strings ts.ps1 really emits plus lowercase, empty, and garbage: ON, UNKNOWN, an unrecognised line, silence, a non-string and a non-zero exit all refuse, and each asserts NOTHING WAS SPAWNED rather than merely that the job errored. This is the failure CLAUDE.md already records once -- `-match 'ON'` does not match UNKNOWN, so a 'not ON means off' test reads an unreadable probe as safe and pastes 102 chunks onto a build plane. Preflight.ok is False on an EMPTY check list too: all([]) is a probe that answers without looking. Preconditions re-run on the worker between the button and the run.

**Building and verifying are two verdicts.** Driving the UI on screen showed the header reading BUILD FAILED beside four written, pasteable slabs, because Forest Church has pre-existing FAIL findings. Now: BUILT / '2 slabs written -- largest 2,514 of 30,720 bytes', then separately VERIFY: FAULTS FOUND / '2 fail / 4 warn / 11 pass' and 'These are findings about the map, not about producing it.' BUILD STOPPED remains for a job that genuinely produced nothing. The findings themselves are unchanged -- still full sentences, still red and first. `ok` rows now start collapsed behind a chip carrying their count, because 20 findings of 200 characters is a wall; fail and warn are never collapsed.

Windows only, said plainly: Driver.available is platform-only, /api/options carries the sentence, the page hides every control rather than offering a dead button, and both POSTs refuse with the same sentence. A non-zero review.ps1 exit is reported and NEVER retried -- a retry stamps a second copy of the map. Shots get their own root (out/flyby, not out_dir) and their own suffix allowlist rather than widening the file endpoint's.

tasks.what: Chat: a sentence becomes a SPEC, and Python builds the slab from it
tasks.note:
BUILT as citysmith/slabchat.py (SlabSpec, SLAB_TOOL, apply_edits/edit -> Turn, build) plus 45 tests. Verified end to end: a 16x12 two-storey tavern builds to 2,718 compressed bytes, 8.8%% of the 30,720 cap, and round-trips through Slab.decode. The worst case the bounds allow (24x24, 3 storeys, cluttered, roofed, min_room 2, 4-tile apron) is 5,631 placements at 49%% of cap, and test_the_largest_legal_spec_fits_in_one_slab re-measures against a 75%% ceiling so anything that adds dressing trips it -- the same re-check rule the town build follows.

**A strict tool schema silently DROPS `minimum`/`maximum`/`multipleOf` rather than rejecting them, so an enum is the only real bound on the wire and a Python clamp is the backstop, not the constraint.** That explains `ai._CITY_TOOL`'s `max_floors: enum [1,2,3,4]`, whose reason was never written down and which a future tidy-up would have 'simplified' back into an unbounded field. test_no_bound_in_the_schema_is_expressed_as_a_numeric_range walks the schema and fails on any of the nine discarded keywords. `seed` is the deliberate exception -- a million-member enum is absurd and no seed can make the result unbuildable -- so there the Python fold is the sole bound.

Degradation is measured, not hoped for: `width: 400` clamps to 24, `kind: 'spaceport'` leaves the field alone, unknown fields are ignored, and non-dict input (string, list, None) returns the spec untouched with one note. apply_edits never raises, so a bad model response gives a boring room rather than a broken one. Offline is PROVEN rather than asserted -- a subprocess sets sys.modules['anthropic'] = None and replaces socket.socket/create_connection with raisers -- and determinism is checked across two subprocesses at different PYTHONHASHSEED, the pattern test_determinism.py established after string-keyed sets shipped a non-reproducible scene.

**What a spec CANNOT say is part of the product.** Fixtures and room names have no injection point in the geometry (see chat-room-vocabulary), so `unsupported` is a REQUIRED array in the schema -- 'nothing was dropped' has to be said as an explicit [], not left as the default of omission -- and Turn keeps `problems` (what Python repaired) apart from `unapplied` (what the generator cannot do at all), because they fail differently. Python never sees the sentence, so only the model can report the second. Turn.summary() prints it under 'Not built -- this generator has no setting for:'.

tasks.what: Chat: edit the spec and rebuild, and be honest that it is not reading the board
tasks.note:
BUILT as citysmith/chatsession.py -- ChatSession over a tuple of Steps, where **the history IS the state**: history[-1].spec is the current spec, so there is no second copy to drift. That is the same rule as 'metrics must read the artifact, not the plan', applied to session state. history[0] is the opening spec, so it is never empty and undo() always has somewhere to land.

**Kept in its own module rather than inside slabchat, deliberately.** slabchat's guarantee is that the generation half is pure and offline, proven in a subprocess with anthropic unimportable and socket.socket replaced by a raiser. The session holds mutable state and shells out to PowerShell; putting subprocess in that file would make 'nothing below slabchat.edit reaches the network' a matter of careful reading rather than a property of a file.

**What it cannot see is a queryable property, not a comment.** ChatSession.blind_spots returns BlindSpot records with a REQUIRED `because` field -- 'cannot read the board' invites somebody to go and make it read the board, so the entry carries the copy-out measurements that say what they would be signing up for. Two standing entries and two more once something has been handed off, including that the board may hold the OLDER build and there is no erase. Three separations are tested: `problems` is what Python repaired, `unapplied` is what the SPEC has no field for, `blind_spots` is what the session cannot know about the WORLD. Undo never unpastes what was handed over.

tasks.what: Send a small slab to the clipboard rather than driving the game
tasks.note:
BUILT as chatsession.to_clipboard / hand_off -- exactly one command, `ts.ps1 setclip`, and nothing else. No click, no keystroke, no camera; the user presses Ctrl+V. A structural test scans the module for all 27 game-driving ts.ps1 verbs and fails on any of them, so the no-synthetic-input property is enforced rather than remembered.

**The base64 cannot go on the command line, and the reason is measured.** WinError 206 fires once the WHOLE command line passes 32,767 chars (the CreateProcess lpCommandLine limit) -- bisected twice at different prefix lengths, 32,588 and 32,711 payload chars, which is how we know the budget is 32,767 minus the command and **shrinks when the repo moves**. The compressed cap is 30,720 bytes = 40,960 base64 chars, so a legal slab exceeds the entire command line. It goes to a mkstemp file that PowerShell reads back instead: 42,000 chars through a 279-char command line, byte-exact, removed in a finally. mkstemp rather than a pid-derived name because the sidecar is a threaded server.

Handoff.text is populated on EVERY path including every failure -- off Windows, no PowerShell, ts.ps1 missing, non-zero exit, timeout -- with how=MANUAL and 'copy the N characters yourself'. A chat that built a good slab and lost it to a missing shell has failed at the last inch. Verified end to end: a 16x12 tavern, 3,624 chars, on the clipboard and read back byte-identical, decoding to 621 placements.

tasks.what: Verify the sidecar on screen at second-monitor proportions
tasks.note:
Driven and screenshotted through the Browser pane, which is the reason the UI is a web page rather than Tkinter. What only a screen can settle: whether the verify report is readable at a glance or a wall of text; whether the chat and the build view can share one column without either being useless; whether it works at a portrait second monitor as well as a landscape one (`resize_window`); and whether it is legible in both light and dark. Same standard as every other review here -- look at it, do not assert about it.

-- PART DONE, and deliberately still open. What is MEASURED: the page is self-sufficient (no asset comes from another origin, so it works offline on a second monitor); both colour schemes are defined and the worst visible contrast is 6.86:1 light and 5.54:1 dark against WCAG AA's 4.5; no horizontal scroll at 420, 900 or 2560 px, so portrait and landscape both reflow. A real build was driven through the page end to end -- Forest Church imported, progress streamed live, 20 findings, chunk table in paste order, reference map and downloads all rendered.

**What is NOT done is the part the task is actually about.** The Browser pane would not composite frames in this session, so no screenshot was ever taken and NOBODY HAS SEEN THIS UI. Contrast ratios cannot answer whether twenty findings of 200 characters read as a report or as a wall, which is the question. Driving it did find two real faults a reading would not have -- the header said BUILD FAILED beside four pasteable slabs, and the pass block was a wall -- and both are fixed; that is evidence the remaining look is worth taking, not that it can be skipped. Evidence is now a capture in docs/images/ so this cannot be closed by assertion.

Evidence is `test_the_sidecar_has_been_looked_at`, which does NOT exist yet -- that is the point. Writing it is part of closing this: it should assert a capture of the running UI exists in docs/images/. A placeholder that merely FAILS does not work here, because `tasks --check` resolves whether a test exists, not whether it passes, so a failing stub reads as evidence and the entry goes stale. Open + evidence missing is the honest state.

tasks.what: Let a caller name rooms and place fixtures, instead of only setting a density
tasks.note: Found while building `slabchat`: the chat spec was designed to carry fixtures, and it cannot, because the geometry API has no injection point for either half. `floorplan.generate` has no `rooms=` parameter and `_ROOM_MENU` is private and keyed on kind, so "a room called the strongroom" is not expressible. `build._dress` picks props from the private `_PROP_CATEGORY` / `_PROP_CATEGORY_BY_KIND` dicts and the only exposed lever is `prop_density`, a float, so "put the bar on the north wall" is not expressible either. `slabchat` therefore translates fixtures to an honest `furnish` enum over that float and REPORTS what it could not apply, rather than silently dropping half a sentence -- which is the failure this project already has a section about. The `ui-chat-modify` note promises wall placement; until this lands, that promise is only kept for the fields the spec really has. Closing it means a public `rooms=` on `generate` and a fixture hint `_dress` can honour, both of which are core-geometry changes and want their own review.

tasks.what: Measure the Campaign Boards filter box, and switch by name if it holds up
tasks.note:
MEASURED 2026-08-26, and the filter holds up. Clicking the box at client (220,163) focuses it and Ctrl+V pastes from the clipboard -- typing still does not work, same as the rename dialog, because TaleSpire reads raw input. Filtering for 'Sedgewater' collapsed a 30-board campaign to the 4 matches, and the documented row arithmetic HELD on the filtered list: rows start at client y=200, 42 apart, play arrow at x=360, expander at x=79. The current board is highlighted in place and shows a person icon where the others show a play arrow, so 'which one am I on' is readable off the shot without counting. What is still unmeasured is the SWITCH itself -- clicking a filtered row's play arrow and confirming the right board loads. **Seen on screen 2026-08-26 and not yet measured.** The Campaign Boards panel carries a `Filter...` box at roughly client (228, 163) on a 1920x1080 window, with a clear `x` at (384, 163). Nothing in this repo mentions it, and it is very likely the answer to the oldest entry in CLAUDE.md's 'Not built yet': *switching to an existing board, unattended*, which is blocked because the list re-sorts on every rename and nothing can read text off the screen -- 'needs either OCR or a keybind we have not found'. A filter needs neither: paste the name, the list narrows, click the first row.

Four things must be measured before anything is built on it, and they are the four that decide whether a row position can be trusted: prefix or substring matching; case sensitivity; whether filtered rows start at the same y=200 as unfiltered ones; and whether the current board's row still expands in place (~134 px) when filtered, since that expansion is what breaks row arithmetic today. Method is a paste, a screenshot, and a diff against the unfiltered shot.

Blocked in the session that found it: driving synthetic clicks into the game was refused by the permission layer, so the box was observed in a screenshot and never operated. Existence is evidence; behaviour is not. Do NOT write `scene.ps1 switch -ByName` on the strength of a screenshot -- this project's own rule is that a probe read from one angle is a probe that lies.

USED LIVE 2026-09-01 for a real switch, East Tradebourne 09-01f -> Forest Church 09-01f. What it adds to the measurements above:
- Pasting '09-01f' into the filter cut the list to exactly the four boards, current one highlighted, rows at the documented y=200+42n. A filtered list IS stable enough to click by row arithmetic.
- **The play arrow needs TWO clicks**: the first lands as hover (the 'Go to board' tooltip appears, nothing switches), the second fires. Same shape as the commit-needs-a-real-hold rule -- budget two clicks in any scripted switch.
- The switch itself then took ~20 s on a 28k-asset board, matching the documented load wait.

tasks.what: The double-right-click centring cannot be driven by ts.ps1 as written
tasks.note:
CLAUDE.md records the community finding that a double RIGHT click centres the camera on the point clicked (measured once: frame moved 39.06, pines centred), and calls it the primitive the planner was missing. DRIVEN 2026-09-01 it does not fire: `ts.ps1 dblrclick` (two raw RDOWN/RUP pairs, 70 ms then 140 ms apart, cursor moved once, 40 ms holds) moved the frame 0.88 against a 0.5 noise floor -- four attempts, in and out of build mode. Two `Press` calls are worse: the 250 ms post-button sleep busts the double-click window entirely.

So either the original measurement was made by hand, or the gesture needs something the synthetic path is not providing -- real pointer MOTION between the clicks is the prime suspect, since that is exactly what carried creatures needed (`mouse_event` motion vs `SetCursorPos`). Next probe: two clicks with a 1 px relative `MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE` between them, and a hand test to confirm the gesture works at all in this build.

Until it fires, the aim route has no self-correcting hop, which is what the Forest Church money-shot attempt spent ~15 frames discovering.

tasks.what: Build a calibration target into every town, at the origin marker
tasks.note:
THE missing piece of the aim route, named precisely by the 2026-09-01 money-shot attempt on Forest Church 09-01f.

Everything else already works and was exercised for real: the UI's camera engine planned the framing (focus (74,76), dist 31.9, pitch 60, cross in frame, 63 px/tile), driving into the measured stops gives dist and pitch BY CONSTRUCTION, `_roof_rings`-style arithmetic gives the zoom tick count, and the rasterised ASCII plan locates any feature in map coordinates. What no tool can supply on a town board is the camera's CURRENT focus and yaw: `camera_read.py` recovers a full pose from one screenshot **of the calibration target**, and a town board has no target. That is `camera-drive-open-loop`'s gap, met on a real errand.

The fix is to make every town its own calibration board: lay the camtarget pattern (or any known asymmetric pattern of cheap tiles) at a KNOWN MAP LOCATION -- beside the origin registration marker is the natural spot, since every chunk already agrees about it -- so `camera_read` works on any pasted town, and `camera_aim --from shot.png` can then emit moves in MAP coordinates. A dozen tiles of cobble in a corner nobody plays on, in exchange for closed-loop camera drives on every board.

Without it, navigation degenerates to flying by scene-reading, which cost six shots on 09-01e and ~15 on this attempt before the stop rule fired both times. The wandering is not a skill problem; it is a missing instrument.

tasks.what: An internal height boundary gets the taller mass's wall
tasks.note:
From the user's close-up on a 09-01f board: an open hole between a lower wing's hip roof and the taller range beside it, interior decking visible through the gap.

**Diagnosed independently twice (subagent and in-line) to the same mechanism**: `_find_perimeters` records an edge only where the neighbouring cell belongs to a DIFFERENT building, so inside one id -- a `building_ranges` two-range house -- and between siblings of one church complex, the boundary has no perimeter edge and the shell pass builds nothing there. The taller storey was a three-sided box open on the junction plane. Measured on a minimal 6x10 two-range house: six junction faces, the span between the lower head (2.5) and taller head (4.5) held NOTHING. `building_ranges`' own docstring carried the false premise -- 'the roof pass needs no changes at all'.

**The fix is the pattern every tile-building game converges on** (the research trail is in the 2026-09-01 session: Sims/Rising World guides say 'build walls the full width of the gap, one brick higher than the roof'; modular tilesets ship dedicated through-roof wall pieces; the academic form is the weighted straight skeleton, where edges start at different heights). Implemented inside the facade loop, which owns the building's dealt fabric: for every cell whose same-mass neighbour stands fewer storeys, lay the face wall on that side for the missing levels. Blind on purpose -- most of it is behind the lower roof's slope.

**Plus the residual the diagnosis named**: `fall` read every off-wing side as downhill (`rings.get(..., -1)`), so the junction course turned its slope over TOWARD the new wall -- the photographed spike. A side into `w_against` is uphill now; the two junction corners became straight slopes (Corner 02 -> Side 03, measured on the slab diff), and the zoomed board shot shows the lower roof dying into the wall as one plane.

Costs, measured: Forest Church +11 assets, tile seams 5,056 -> 5,082 (the roof lapping the new wall, the deliberate-overlap class). The nave/chancel junction gets NO wall, correctly: `building_ranges` drops the nave's far end to the chancel's own height so they meet flush -- pinned by `test_a_flush_junction_gets_no_through_roof_wall`, after the first check misread 0 as a failure.

THE PASTED 09-01f BOARDS PREDATE THIS FIX and show the hole; the next rebuild carries it.

tasks.what: Make ts.ps1 boards read HUD state instead of pressing Space blind
tasks.note:
`boards` sends `Space` blind, and `Space` is a TOGGLE -- so with the panel already up it closes the HUD and the follow-up click lands on whatever is behind it. The command's own return string admits this ('CHECK THE SHOT'), which is a documented unreliability standing in for a fix. It has failed twice and worked once.

Observed 2026-08-26: run against an already-open panel, the current board changed from Pelvesthollow to Unknown Realm 22 across the call. Whether the call did it or a human at the keyboard did is NOT established -- the game was live and unattended-driving was stopped at that point per the skill's own first rule -- so this is a reason to fix the blind toggle, not a measurement of what it does.

The fix is a HUD-state probe shaped like `planestate`, and it inherits planestate's whole warning: aim at a widget that exists ONLY when the HUD is up (the panel's 'Campaign Boards' title bar, or the Filter box), derive its position from the client rect rather than hardcoding, and return UNKNOWN rather than guessing. Reading the board and calling it a state has happened three times in this project -- planestate on Graybank's grass, the toolbar centring, the elevation track scanned from the wrong window edge -- and twice the wrong toggle was pressed as a result. Then: press Space only when the HUD is down, and never click a row without a fresh screenshot taken after the panel is confirmed open.

-- DONE as ts.ps1 `hudstate` / `boardsstate` plus a rewritten `boards`. **It was unsafe, not just unreliable, and the reason is that there are THREE states where the old code saw two.** HUD down + panel closed: Space raises it. HUD UP + panel closed: Space HIDES it and the click that follows lands on the board, in build mode, where a click is not a no-op. That is what put two stray clicks on a live board while investigating this. `boards` now reads both, presses Space only when the HUD is actually down, does NOTHING when the panel is already open (it used to toggle itself shut), and refuses on any unreadable state instead of clicking.

**Both probes are self-calibrating, and that is the transferable part.** The naive shape -- sample one patch, call dark pixels 'the widget' -- has now failed three times here: Graybank's grass fooled planestate, and MY FIRST CUT of this probe read the left tool column and reported OPEN at a closed panel, which is how the second stray click happened. Each probe measures its widget against a control patch of board, so a dark board darkens both and the DIFFERENCE stays near zero. Measured across real frames: panel open 77.3 / 84.1 / 84.6 vs closed -6.9; HUD up 81.6 / 81.8 vs down -0.1 / 0.0. The band between is nobody's measurement and returns `unknown`.

Also corrected the command's own return string, which still carried the refuted 'current board's row is expanded ~134px' claim after the comment and the skill had been fixed -- a correction is not done until every copy of the claim moves.

tasks.what: Separate workshop boards from publish-ready ones, using folders
tasks.note:
**Folders make the campaign split unnecessary, and that is measured rather than assumed.** The row expander (x=79) opens exactly three items -- Delete board, Set Folder, Reload Board -- and there is NO 'move to campaign'. So splitting across campaigns means copying or re-pasting every board, while splitting across folders is one dialog. Verified end to end on a throwaway board 2026-08-26: Set Folder opens 'Move to folder', free text creates one, and the board is filed under a collapsible `Workshop` heading that sorts ABOVE the ungrouped boards. It is a move, not a copy -- no second board afterwards.

That also blunts two other problems at once: twenty-one `Unknown Realm N` rows collapse to one foldable line, and a board's folder is a second, coarser label in a list whose only other signal is a name clipped at about two dozen characters.

What is left to build is the bookkeeping, not the mechanism. `Registry` already carries a `campaign` field that nothing sets; a `folder` beside it would let `boards prune` say 'unnamed AND in Ready to publish' -- which should be a hard error rather than a LOOK FIRST, because a board nobody named has no business in the published set. Deciding what belongs in which folder is still a person's call: nothing here can read a board's contents.

-- DESIGN CHARACTERISED 2026-08-26, on throwaway boards. **A folder is not an object you create.** It exists only while at least one board is in it: name one and it appears, move the last board out and it is GONE -- measured, `Workshop` vanished the moment its only board was filed elsewhere. Two consequences for any plan: you cannot pre-create `Ready to publish` and then fill it, and there is no folder rename, so renaming means re-filing every board under the new name.

Folders sort alphabetically among themselves and above every ungrouped board, and each collapses to one row. The dropdown lists `- NO FOLDER -` first, so filing is reversible; a board is in at most one folder and the move leaves no second board.

**The row menu is shorter for a board you are not standing on** -- Reload Board is current-board only -- so Set Folder is at row+68 normally and row+63 on the current board. And folders BREAK row arithmetic: a header eats a slot, an expanded folder inserts children, an expanded menu inserts two or three more. The 42 px pitch holds but the Nth-board-to-y mapping does not; read the shot.

Unresolved: the icon at the folder header's far right (x~378, a figure in a dashed circle) shows no tooltip on hover and has not been clicked.

-- DONE. The campaign is two collapsed folders: `Ready to publish` holds the three towns and the two tracked interiors, `Workshop` holds everything else -- 29 boards down to two rows, nothing left loose. Filed with `ts.ps1 setfolder`, added for this, because 27 boards by hand is hundreds of clicks next to a Delete board item.

**The loop needed one non-obvious step: the target folder AUTO-EXPANDS when a board lands in it**, and the filed board's own row menu stays open, so a naive loop files the wrong boards from the second one on. Collapse the target again and the geometry returns exactly -- headers at 200 and 241, first ungrouped board at 283 -- so file-at-283, collapse, repeat has a stationary target.

On the bookkeeping side: `boards.parse_seen` reads a listing indented the way the panel draws it, and `unfit_to_publish` makes 'unnamed AND in the published folder' a HARD ERROR with a non-zero exit, where the same board loose in the campaign is only a LOOK FIRST. Filing something under `Ready to publish` is a claim; `Unknown Realm N` is the name the game invents when nobody made one; the two contradict each other, and the likeliest cause is a click that missed by one row.

**The listing format is indentation and not `Folder/Name`, and that is not a style choice.** This project's own board scheme is `GRB/T14 The Halfling and the Fox Interior`, so a slash-separated listing files it under a folder called `GRB` and the published set reads as empty -- silently, which is the failure mode this repo keeps records of. The first cut of the parser did exactly that and a test caught it.

-- FOLLOW-UP: **the board named `Pelvesthollow` was the STALE build, and the good one was sitting unnamed in the workshop.** Flown and compared 2026-08-26. The old board is a single thatch roof material, one narrow path, no fences, no yards and no props; the rebuild has two roof materials, fenced yards, mixed paving with a stone patch at the crossroads, and dressing. That is exactly the 2026-08-25 change list, so the comparison decides itself rather than resting on taste. Swapped: the rebuild is now `Pelvesthollow` in Ready to publish, the old one is `Pelvesthollow (old)` in Workshop. Nothing deleted -- there is no erase, and the old board is still where its history is.

Worth noticing what this says about the folders: the published set was WRONG on the day it was created, and it was wrong in the way a name cannot show. `Ready to publish` is a claim somebody has to make by looking, which is why `unfit_to_publish` only checks the one thing a machine can see -- that the board has a name at all.

But --fence-style palisade then built the outlying farms' boundaries as ten-foot stockades across a wheat field, so the style is chosen per run by the same closed-versus-open test. Tiles lay on CELLS: laying them along a bearing put 166 off the half-tile grid.

tasks.what: Delete probe boards from the campaign, driven
tasks.note:
MEASURED end to end 2026-08-26 -- 34 `Unknown Realm` probe boards removed by hand-driven clicks -- but NOT yet a command, which is why this is open. The procedure: row EXPANDER at x=90, `Delete board` at row+38, click at x=160. That opens a TYPED confirmation -- 'Type DELETE below to confirm' -- so the field at (960,551) must be focused and the word pasted (Ctrl+V; typing never works, TaleSpire reads raw input), then OK at (830,605). A 'Board deleted' toast confirms. That dialog is why an accidental delete is essentially impossible, and it is worth knowing before anyone builds a loop.

Two geometry traps. With the list at rest rows are 42 apart, and deleting the top one leaves the NEXT board at the same y -- so a loop can reuse one coordinate. But the sections re-flow: once Workshop emptied, y=406 stopped being a probe board and became a Sedgewater row, and the ungrouped section below Workshop starts at y=581. Re-read the list between batches; never reuse a coordinate across a section change.

FILTERED ROWS CANNOT BE EXPANDED. The filter renders a bullet where the unfiltered list renders an expander, and clicking it does nothing -- so the filter finds boards but cannot delete them, and the filter has to be cleared first. That is the constraint `board-filter-switch` did not know.

tasks.what: Size a yard from the ground the building actually has, per side
tasks.note: YARD_REACH was one number for every building in every town. The reach is now measured per side from the open ground out that way, capped in front of the door, so a farmstead gets a full yard and a terrace house gets a back one. Yard sizes across East Tradebourne run 5-197 cells against a flat 49.

tasks.what: Keep the frontage shallow and put the ground round the back
tasks.note: Back deeper than front on 205 of East Tradebourne's 228 yards (90%); door side mean reach 1.25 against 3.50 opposite.

tasks.what: Step the yard boundary at FENCE_MODULE instead of at the cell
tasks.note: Runs are chained and stepped at the panel's own length; an odd run leaves the remainder as a gap mid-run rather than lapping a panel. Pelvesthollow 599 panels -> 312 with bigger yards, collinear laps 507 -> 0, panels in a road 27 -> 0, inside a wall 0 -> 0.

tasks.what: Stop the 2x2 terrain block laying grass over an agreed yard role

tasks.what: Measure a boundary piece where it stands, not where its coordinate is
tasks.note: A standing [FAIL] on Sedgewater under EVERY fence style -- 2 pieces at x=145.00, z=134.00 for eight of them, 7 for palisade -- and nothing was standing in a street. Both boundary checks read the placement's stored coordinate as the collider CENTRE. It is the asset's ORIGIN: on a prop that is the centre, on a tile it is the collider's min corner, which is the distinction `build.placed_bounds` exists to hold and every other placement check in verify already goes through. Every boundary asset in the medieval palette is a prop except the two palisade pieces (off=(0.5,0.5)), and the enclosure ring is built from those whatever --fence-style asks for -- so the box came out half a cell low on both axes, straddled the four cells meeting at the tile's own corner, and caught a street two cells away. That is why drystone and hedge, which share no piece, reported the identical count at the identical coordinate; it was never the fence kit. MEASURED: with the offset applied, 0 intruding pieces on all 9 styles, and the map check's 2 off-map pieces on the Pinfold golden were inside it all along. The laying passes were right; only the reading was wrong. Caught in passing and fixed with it: _lay_fences tested a JOINT against the one cell its centre landed in while testing a PANEL against its body -- harmless for the 0.51 stone post, not for the 1.64 `paling` corner, which spans four cells. No piece moved on Sedgewater (fence_pieces identical across all 8 styles).

tasks.what: Place a kit's feature panels by rule, never by rate
tasks.note: Twenty-five feature panels exist beyond wall and window: 12 arch, 2 alcove, 2 breach, 5 ruin, 3 Ship decor, 2 porthole, 2 supported, 1 shield, 1 prison cage. **Most of them are OPENINGS, not decoration.** Read at 1-in-4 on `PROBE wall variance`: the Dungeon Cellar and MegaDungeon runs are see-through, with grass visible through the wall -- correct for a ruin, ruinous on a house. An arch belongs where the raster already says there is a way through (a gate, a passage under a building, a market arcade); a breach or a ruin belongs to a building the map has decided is ruined. Moorgoth's alcoves are recesses rather than holes and its LIT alcove and LIT arches carry their own light, which is the one piece here that would light a street with no lamp props at all.

tasks.what: Wall stairs on Forest Church stand over nothing
tasks.note: MEASURED, and it was neither hypothesis. The flight's own fill is correct, and the border taper is nowhere near it -- (80, 88) and (81, 88) sit in the middle of a 187x180 map. The cause is two correct passes disagreeing about what a placement covers. `_lay_terrain` sheets open country in 2x2 blocks; `_lay_npc_marks` runs last and *clears* the cell it marks, because a mark that covers the ground rather than replacing it is two coplanar surfaces and a person arriving inside a barrel. `Builder.clear_cells` identifies a placement by its collider centre, which for a 2x2 block is one of its four cells -- so a guard post at (81, 89) deleted the whole `Grass - Lush` block laid at (80, 88) and stripped the ground from three cells that had no post on them. Forest Church: 53 posts took up six blocks, orphaning eighteen cells of which fifteen were left with no ground at all, and the only two anyone could see were under the rampart stair. `_lay_terrain` now takes a `reserved` set and refuses to fuse a quad holding a cell a later pass will take back. 3 floating placements -> 0 and 15 ground holes -> 0, for 44 extra tiles in 28,586. The same trap is written up for yards in `build_from_tilemap` and was solved there by deciding the material once instead of clearing and re-laying; a mark cannot do that, because clearing is also how it takes the props out of the cell.

tasks.what: Frame probe boards with the camera model instead of blind fly holds
tasks.note: `panel_review.ps1` asks `camera_aim.py --slab` before it pastes and prints whether the whole slab will be in shot. `camera_aim.py --slab` is new: it reads a slab's ground extent through `build.placed_bounds`, so a review is never told how big the thing it is looking at is. **It reports and does not drive**, deliberately: `camera-drive-open-loop` is open against a driven move landing 14 degrees off in yaw, so the model is trusted to say what a frame holds and not yet to steer. Open-loop needs no calibration target here because the script already drives into both measured stops -- 200 scroll ticks and 250 px of pitch each exceed the range -- so the pose before -Oblique is dist_max and pitch_max by construction. That was true by accident before this and is now the reason. WHAT IT FOUND IMMEDIATELY: none of the three wall probe boards can be photographed whole. 53x45 all-kits needs 95 tiles of slant range, 41x29 variance needs 62, 53x5 in-use needs 60, against a stop at 49.75. Four exchanges of flying in the session that prompted this were spent on boards that were never framable. CAUGHT IN PASSING, not fixed: `Framing.covered` is an overlap against `visible_bounds`, the axis-aligned box round the frustum, so on a wide shallow slab it reads 1.00 while `covers_all` puts 0 of 4 corners in shot. Both are right about different things, but a caller must not print it beside a 'too big' headline. Pinned by test_covered_is_a_bounds_overlap_and_not_a_corner_count.

tasks.what: Preview the frame in 3D, and drag it with the game's own controls
tasks.note: The board projected through the SAME Camera that plans the move, returned as screen-space quads; the browser draws them and does no 3D. Dragging runs the rig server-side, so the sensitivities and the STOPS are the measured ones -- the preview cannot show a shot the camera cannot take, and it says so when it is against a stop. 93 ms a frame before the camera basis was hoisted out of the per-corner projection and boxes were rejected on their centre; 4-7 ms after, on a 991-building town.

tasks.what: Explain why a driven move landed 14 degrees off in yaw
tasks.note: `/api/camera/drive` ran its four moves and the camera moved, but it landed at yaw 164.25 against a planned 150.06 and pitch 41.41 against 44.94. NOT a gain error: re-measured immediately afterwards on the same board, a DX=100 drag gave 0.1858 deg/px and DX=400 gave 0.1879, both matching the calibrated 0.18761, so the sensitivity is right at both magnitudes. Yaw came up short and pitch overshot, which rules out a single scale factor. Two candidates, neither tested: the plan's `fly d 0.37` is well outside the 0.08-0.14 s the WASD ramp was measured over, and the final pose sits at a 37-tile range where the reader's own envelope note says a near mark can outrank a far one. Four earlier moves driven through camera_aim.ps1 landed within 0.9 deg, so this is a real regression in a specific case and not the general behaviour.

tasks.what: Deal a whole wall FABRIC per building, not one kit per tier
tasks.note: `walls.TIER_FABRICS` gives each tier a weighted set of roles and `walls.fabric_for` deals one per building, stably, the way the wall variant used to be. Wired into `build_from_tilemap`. A/B on Forest Church with TIER_FABRICS emptied: Abandoned Village walls 0 -> 72, Tavern 521 -> 464, Rural 79 -> 63, 6 of 51 buildings changed fabric, total placements 28,540 -> 28,539. TWO THINGS THE WIRING FORCED. `glazes` is a flag now rather than `glass = None`: utility was kept blind by having no window, and a fabric can bring its own (Rural has one), so dealing fabrics would have glazed every barn -- test_a_barn_gets_no_glass_however_glazed_its_fabric_is. And where a fabric is chosen the palette's pieces are the WRONG kit by construction, so the fallbacks re-point at the fabric's own and stay None where it has none; `glass` takes only the 1-cell window, because it is used as a single-segment fallback and a 2-cell piece in one cell overhangs. THE ROOF FOLLOWS, in one case only. Roofs are dealt independently on purpose (ROOF_MIX exists so a quarter is not monochrome), but a building clad in the `poor` fabric is authored damaged and the pack ships the match: `roof_side_slate` is `Haunted roof 1x1`, the same Abandoned Village kit. tasks.note: F9 opens Cutscene Mode's camera editor, which shows Camera Speed and Rotation Sensitivity -- both 1.0 when config/camera.json was calibrated, and both user settings. tasks.what: Size a probe board to what the camera can actually photograph
tasks.note: Every probe tool here picks its grid by eye -- `wallkit_board.py` defaults to 4 columns, `wallrun_probe.py` to 3 -- and none of them knows the camera stops pulling back at 49.75 tiles of slant range, which is about 50x27 tiles in one shot. Measured: the all-kits board at 53x45 needs 95. The tools already compute their own extent and `camera.frame_rect` already answers the question, so a probe should either choose its column count to fit or emit a shot list and say how many frames it will take. tasks.what: Move the focus by double-right-clicking, not by flying
tasks.note: Measured: a double RIGHT click centres the camera on the clicked point (frame moved 39.06 against a 0.42 noise floor; a double LEFT click at the same pixel does nothing). `plan` currently translates the focus with WASD `fly` legs, and the ramp is only measured over 0.08-0.14 s -- the one driven move that landed 14 degrees out used a 0.37 s leg. Replacing the fly legs with project-then-click removes the ramp from the plan entirely and is self-correcting: you click where the model believes the point is, so a model error shows up as a landing error you can measure.

tasks.what: Report a hole in the ground, not just something standing over one
tasks.note: `floating_placements` only fires when something happens to be standing on a missing tile. Measured while fixing `stairs-floating`: Forest Church had 15 cells the tilemap gives ground to and the placements do not, and 13 of them were INVISIBLE to the build report; East Tradebourne had 54, of which 52 were invisible. The FAIL that found the bug fired only because a rampart stair happened to stand on one of the two. That is the 'metrics must read the artifact' family exactly -- the check reads the consequence rather than the condition. A pass comparing placements against the tilemap for missing ground catches the class directly, and it returns 0 on both towns now, so it can be added clean rather than as a new failing check.

tasks.what: Chase the order-dependent tile-seam count between the UI and the CLI
tasks.note: `test_the_build_endpoint_returns_the_same_findings_as_the_cli` has failed in a full run for two independent observers on 2026-08-28, with `tile seams: 123` from the UI against `274` from the CLI. It passes in isolation, passes with test_pipeline.py alongside, and passes on re-run. **I first attributed this to two sessions writing the tree at once and that explanation is probably wrong**: a subagent saw it in its own run with a stable tree, and concurrent writes would not produce two self-consistent but different seam counts. Order-dependent state somewhere -- a module-level cache is the obvious suspect, and `build._WALL_FAMILIES` is keyed on `id(catalog)`, which CPython reuses after a catalog is garbage collected. That is a specific, checkable hypothesis and it has not been tested. || 2026-08-28: the suspected cause was found and FIXED, but the flake is not confirmed closed because it was never reproduced on demand. `build.wall_families` cached `id(catalog) -> families` and held no reference to the catalog, so a collected catalog could hand its address to the next one and the second would be served the first's families. Now keyed with a `weakref.finalize` that drops the entry when the catalog dies (`Catalog` is an unhashable dataclass, so WeakKeyDictionary is not available), pinned by test_the_family_cache_cannot_serve_a_dead_catalogs_families. Leave this OPEN until the uiserver test has run green in full suites for a while: the aliasing was real and mine, but nothing has shown it was THIS flake's cause.

tasks.what: Gable the ends of a great building instead of hipping them
tasks.note: WIRED into `_lay_roofs`. A wing asks its QUARTER how to end its ridge (`_wing_gable` -> `gable_end_for`), and `_lay_gabled_wing` builds it from `roof_courses` with the ridge along the wing's long axis. Three gates keep it honest: `quarter_at` is None on a settlement whose kinds do not cluster -- which is most of them -- and then every wing is hipped exactly as before; a wing under GABLE_MIN_RIDGE/GABLE_MIN_SPAN has no ridge to terminate and stays hipped; and `crow` falls back to `flush` where the fabric ships no half-height wall, which is every medieval kit but Castle Fortified and Marble Palace. MEASURED A/B at seed 33: Pelvesthollow and Graybank are placement-for-placement IDENTICAL (no quarters), while East Tradebourne moves 396,500 -> 397,286 with hip corners collapsing into slopes (Thatched Roof Corner 4040 -> 152, Village Roof Corner 2052 -> 48) and 388 crow treads appearing in the civic quarter. THE REGRESSION THE A/B CAUGHT: the first cut placed no chimney on a gabled wing, taking the town from 1,578 chimneys to 40 -- and nothing in `verify` would have caught it, because every chimney that remained was correct. Guarded by test_a_gabled_wing_still_gets_its_chimney. PASTED AND LOOKED AT 2026-08-29, and the board found two things the file could not. (1) **Cropping a town destroys its quarters, and the gable is keyed on them.** `quarter_map` needs a clustering lift of 1.2; a 44x40 crop of East Tradebourne has 14 buildings and a lift of 1.04, so it has no quarters and every ridge is hipped. That crop was pasted and read as 'the gable did not fire' when the region could not contain it -- the exact failure `feature_report` exists for, on a feature added after it was written. Measured: the same town needs a 160x160 crop, 193 buildings, before its quarters survive. `feature_report` now carries a `gabled ends` line so this cannot be silent again. (2) **A flush gable leaves an open triangle**, measured on guildhall-0001: wall head 6.5, ridge roof 8.0, so a 1.5-tile hole at each end tapering to nothing at the eaves. Closing it needs a wall piece exactly one course tall, and **Tavern and Rural ship none** -- the house and the barn cannot gable at the single-course scale at all, which is the 'only Tavern ships an end piece' shortfall arriving from the other side. Gated: a wing whose fabric has no infill stays hipped, so the board is correct rather than holed. Cost: gables drop from 74%% of wings to 1%% (16 of 1391), all civic. See gable-single-course-infill.
