DONE 2026-09-01. `ONE_VOLUME_KINDS`, `ONE_VOLUME_COURSES` and `is_one_volume` in build.py.

**The diagnosis in the original note was half wrong, and the half that was wrong is the interesting half.** It said a temple was "three courses of Castle Fortified glazed one-in-2 at the front on EVERY course, with upper decks on the interior cells". Measured on Forest Church: `storeys_of` returned **1** for the temple, so the nave was ONE course -- 10 ft to the eaves, the same as the 12-cell shed -- and the facade deck loop, which runs `range(1, storeys)`, laid nothing at all. All 108 upper-floor tiles came from `_lay_towers`, which decks every tower cell at each of its `TOWER_EXTRA_STOREYS` stages: 36 x 3 = 108, exactly. A bell tower HAS stages with floors in them, so those are correct and are still built.

So the church was not a tenement with a tower on it. It was a **hut with a tower on it**, and the tower was doing all the work: read across the whole slab the eaves measured 40 ft, which is the tower, not the nave.

The fix is the one `docs/great-buildings.md` §2 asks for -- "a single storey pitched at 3-4 courses rather than three storeys of two". `storeys_of` returns `ONE_VOLUME_COURSES` (3) for a one-volume kind, which is a COURSE count in a storey count's slot. That is deliberate and it is why nothing else had to change: `storeys_of` is the one number the shell, the upper floors and the roof all read, so the wall grows to three courses, the roof seats on its head by the same arithmetic as every other building, and the tower starts above it. What stops three courses becoming three storeys is the deck guard and the glazing guard, both keyed on `is_one_volume`.

Forest Church, before -> after: nave eaves 10 ft -> 30 ft, ridge (whole envelope) 50 ft -> 70 ft, glazing one low band -> one band at each range's head course, upper-floor tiles inside the nave 0 -> 0 (they were always the tower's). `building_ranges` splits the 102-cell footprint 72/30, so the far end now stands a course lower -- an accidental chancel, and the reason `church-nave-and-chancel` is the natural next one.

**Only `temple` is in the set**, though §2 says the halls are one open storey too. A guildhall here is a tolbooth -- §1.4 wants an arcade below and a civic chamber over, which genuinely has a floor; a manor is a dwelling and a barracks a dormitory. The hall volume is `great-volume-not-floors`, and it is about course counts rather than about deleting floors.

Cost: `tile_seams` 572 -> 580 on Forest Church, from the taller nave. The 7 prop overlaps and 37 boundary corner joins in that report are PRE-EXISTING -- identical with the feature switched off in-process.

PASTED AND LOOKED AT 2026-09-01, on two boards with one camera (`panel_review.ps1`, `CHURCH before2` / `CHURCH after`, crop 100,103,12,24). The profile is the shot that settles it: before, a crenellated keep with a low sprawling barn attached, its nave roof sitting almost on the ground over a single course of wall; after, a silhouette that steps tower -> nave -> lower range, with real masonry under the nave roof.

**Two shots out of three were misleading, and in the way this project keeps re-learning.** `panel_review.ps1` takes plan, oblique and low at ONE yaw, and on this crop that yaw looks straight down the length of the building -- so the 6x6 tower stands directly in front of the 7-wide nave and hides it. Both shots read as a featureless 60 ft stone cliff and I had begun writing up the change as a regression. One `orbit -DX 480` showed the step. A probe read from one angle is a probe that lies, and a three-shot panel at one yaw is one angle.

Worth fixing in the tool rather than remembering: `panel_review.ps1` should take a profile as well, or take a yaw. Filed as `review-cardinal-faces`, which already exists and is now motivated by a real misread rather than by principle.

tasks.what: A church's height comes from its footprint, not from a constant
tasks.note:
MEASURED 2026-09-01 across the five layouts on disk: temples run 30 to 102 cells, a factor of 3.4, and all seven were built to the SAME height -- three courses and a three-stage tower. A 30-cell chapel and a 102-cell town church are not the same building.

| town | id | cells | plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forest Church | temple-0002 | 102 | 6x19 |
| East Tradebourne | temple-0027 | 88 | 8x12 |
| East Tradebourne | temple-0004 | 81 | 10x9 |
| Graybank | temple-0123 | 65 | 15x5 |
| East Tradebourne | temple-0003 | 65 | 15x5 |
| Sedgewater | temple-0006 | 52 | 8x7 |
| East Tradebourne | temple-0991 | 30 | 4x9 |

`CHURCH_BANDS` deals (nave courses, tower stages) from the footprint: chapel 2/3, parish 3/4, town 4/5, great 5/6. The tower scales FASTER than the nave on purpose -- its job is to be the thing seen from across the board, and a tower growing in step never gains on a ridge that is itself growing.

**The house ceiling does not clamp a church, and that is the load-bearing decision.** `--storeys` defaults to 3, so a great church would otherwise lose two of its five courses to a cap that exists to stop cottages reading as towers. A church is the one building whose job is to out-top the town. Bounded by the measured table instead.

PASTED. Forest Church's temple went 3 courses / 6-course tower -> 5 courses / 11-course tower; in its own crop it now stands about two and a half times its neighbour and the tower leaves the frame. `tools/church_probe.py` lays the measured footprints in a row.

**A great church can no longer be photographed in one frame** -- 58 tiles of slant range needed against the measured 50-tile cap. That is a fact about the camera rather than a fault, but it means any future church review is a shot list.

tasks.what: Cap a church tower with a spire from the tall-roof family
tasks.note:
PROBED 2026-09-01, and **the premise was wrong**. This note said a spire was 'a roof set swap rather than new geometry' because `rise` is already read off `side_piece.size_y`. It is not, and the rotation is not the blocker either.

The pieces are real: `Castle Fortified` ships `Tall 2x2x4`, `Tall 2x2x4 Corner in`, `Corner out`, `corner out unique`, `corner round`, `Tall 1x1x4` (1x4x2), `Tall 1x1x2` and two fillers, all under `group='Roof tall'`. Read as renders they are steep shingled planes with carved finials -- spire material.

Built as a sweep (four 6x6 towers, one per quarter turn, `out/spire/sweep.slab.txt`) and pasted on `PROBE spire turns`: **not one of the four closes.** Every bay is a cluster of four separate steep peaks with open undersides showing, and they differ from each other only in which way the jumble faces. That is not a rotation failure -- a wrong turn gives fins in a rank, and exactly one turn closes. This gives four wrong answers.

**The cause is SCALE.** The pieces are 2 cells wide; `_roof_rings` steps ONE cell per ring. So each course lays 2-cell pieces on 1-cell centres and every piece overlaps its neighbour, which is why a 6x6 comes out as four peaks instead of one point. This is the same double-scale problem `roof-2x2-pieces` and `roofrot-wide-scale` solved for the ordinary wide roof family, and the spire needs that path rather than the 1-cell one.

So the order is: reach the double-scale ring path first, THEN sweep the rotation on it. Sweeping the rotation on the 1-cell path was measuring the wrong thing, and it took a board to see that -- the collider drawings in the review page show the bulk correctly and cannot show that the pieces overlap.

Still the biggest remaining lever on 'does it read as a church': a spire says church at a distance where a window cannot be seen.

**DONE 2026-09-01, and the user settled it with a hand-build.** After the sweep above failed on all four turns I had concluded the cause was SCALE -- 2-cell pieces on 1-cell rings. That was wrong too. The slab the user laid (`tests/fixtures/handbuilt_spire.slab`) is **four `Tall 2x2x4 Corner out` on a 4x4, one per quadrant, and NO SLOPE PIECES AT ALL**:

    (0,0) NW rot 12    (2,0) NE rot 6
    (0,2) SW rot 18    (2,2) SE rot 0

Those are exactly `ROOF_CORNER_ROT` plus Castle Fortified's own corner offset of 0 -- all four, no exceptions. **The rotation table we already had described the spire correctly the whole time.** What was wrong was building it out of the wrong pieces and then sweeping a rotation to fix that, which is measuring the wrong thing carefully. Third time on this project that asking for the slab a person laid beat another sweep.

`build.lay_spire` centres a fixed 4x4 cap on the tower, which is not a simplification: a broach spire IS narrower than its tower, and on a 6x6 the one-cell margin left round it is exactly where `_lay_towers` already puts the parapet -- crenellations with a spire rising out of them rather than two features fighting for one ring.

One thing it caught on the way: `spire_piece` first read the building's ROOF kit and found nothing, because `ROOF_MIX` deals roofs independently so the civic roof is Tavern terracotta while the civic wall is Castle Fortified. A spire is masonry continuing upward, so it follows the stone it stands on.

tasks.what: A lower roof meeting a taller wall needs a valley, not an overlap
tasks.note:
PREDICTED by the generator-design review of the plans, then SEEN on the board. Pasted `out/plans2/cruciform.slab.txt` on `PLAN cruciform`: from overhead, every junction where a lower volume meets a taller one carries loose roof pieces standing proud of the wall they run into -- clearest where the transepts meet the crossing and where the chancel meets it.

Each volume is its own building id, so `_lay_roofs` hips each one against its OWN footprint and knows nothing about the wall on the far side of the join. Its eaves course therefore runs straight into the taller masonry instead of dying into a valley, and the pieces that should have been omitted are left sticking out.

This is the price of 'a church complex is several abutting building ids' and it was called in advance: per-bid hips are right, but a lower roof meeting a taller wall has no valley and buries into it. It is the same class of problem as the doubled walls in `church-volumes-break-four-passes`, and probably wants the same fix -- a parent map, so a roof pass can see the sibling volumes it abuts.

Confirmed working on the same paste, so the review had good news too: the **spire closes**. Four corner pieces meet at a point with the finial on top, exactly as the hand-build laid it.

DONE 2026-09-01, PARTIALLY, and the numbers say which part.

`_roof_rings` takes an `against` set: ground the block abuts a TALLER neighbour on, which is not an eave. A side running into masonry has no edge to shed off, so the roof keeps rising and dies into the wall -- that is a valley. Left as a frontier, the flood starts an eaves course there instead, the slope turns over and sheds TOWARDS the wall, and its underside and the ridge pieces that had nothing to lap onto stand proud of the masonry.

Computed once per roof block rather than per wing, so it is not a church special case: a block is a set of cells at one storey count, and anything at a higher one is a wall this block's roof may have to die into. A two-storey house beside a one-storey one had the same defect and nobody had looked. Mapped onto the wing's own 2x2 lattice at the double scale the way `coarse_blocks` maps the wing.

**Measured, roof pieces overhanging a DIFFERENT and taller volume:**

| plan | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| cruciform | 13 | **7** |
| aisled | 8 | 8 |
| narthex | 6 | 6 |
| minster | 1 | 1 |

So it fixes the plan with the most junctions and does nothing for the other three, because their residue is a DIFFERENT mechanism: not an eave facing the wrong way but a piece whose collider box extends past its own cell into the neighbour. Seven `haunted roof corner out tip`, two `corner out` and one `1x1` across the set. That wants clipping at the volume boundary and risks holes, so it is `church-roof-pieces-overhang-the-join` and not this.

**And the nave+chancel church did not need this at all** -- measured before changing anything, its join was already slope/cap/slope with the ridge running straight into the nave. The defect I photographed was on the five-volume cruciform PLAN, and I nearly fixed the wrong building: the first A/B showed 793 placements and 388 seams identical either way, which reads as 'the change does nothing' and actually meant 'this church never had the bug'.

PASTED on `VALLEY on`. Against the earlier shot the transept roofs now run valleys into the crossing instead of scattering loose pieces at every junction.

**CORRECTION, same day: the 'residue' quoted above is not real.** The before/after table (13 -> 7 and so on) counted cells a box merely touches at its far edge, not cells it occupies -- see `church-roof-pieces-overhang-the-join`, withdrawn. Re-measured with `placement_cells`, roof pieces intruding on a taller neighbour are **0 both before and after this change**.

So what did the valley actually buy? 46 placements move on the cruciform -- slopes and flat caps become corner pieces at the junctions -- and the overhead shot is visibly cleaner. That is a real improvement in FORM and the change is right on its own terms: a side running into masonry is not an eave. But the numeric case made for it was measuring nothing, and the honest claim is the picture plus the argument, not the table.

tasks.what: WITHDRAWN: the overhang was a measurement error, not a defect
tasks.note:
**WITHDRAWN 2026-09-01, THE SAME DAY IT WAS FILED. The defect does not exist, and it was my measurement that was wrong.**

The check counted the cells a placement's box covers with `range(int(x0), int(x1) + 1)`. That is a CLOSED range over a HALF-OPEN box: a piece at x=5.0 that is 1.0 wide spans 5.0 to 6.0 and occupies cell 5 only, but the range yields 5 and 6, so every piece was credited with a cell it merely touches at its far edge. Re-measured with `build.placement_cells`, the count across all four plans is **0, before and after the valley fix**. All 28 reported overhangs were the off-by-one.

The tell was in the evidence and I filed it anyway: the breakdown said the offenders were mostly 1x1 pieces with a 1.0x1.0 box after rotation, and a 1x1 box cannot overhang anything. I read past it because the count went down when the valley landed, which made the number look like it was measuring something real.

**Checked for the opposite failure too, since a fix by dropping pieces would have traded a seam for a hole**: every building cell on all four plans is roofed. 0 unroofed of 227, 312, 266 and 308.

Three things kept rather than deleted:
- `build.placement_cells` -- the box-to-cells conversion written down once, because doing it by hand is what invented this.
- `test_placement_cells_does_not_count_the_cell_a_box_merely_touches`.
- `test_no_roof_piece_occupies_a_taller_neighbours_cell` and `test_every_building_cell_is_roofed`, asserted TOGETHER so that a future overhang fix cannot ship a hole as its cure.

And the research the withdrawal came out of: the standard algorithm for this is the **straight skeleton**, and `_roof_rings` is already a grid form of it -- flooding inward one cell at a time IS shrinking the outline at a constant rate, and the ring index is the offset distance. A reflex corner is the skeleton's split event, which `roof_wings` already sidesteps by cutting the plan into maximal rectangles; an edge shared with something taller simply does not propagate, which is what `against` does. So it was already solved in the literature and the code was most of the way there.

tasks.what: A church of several volumes is several SEALED ROOMS
tasks.note:
**The worst thing about the multi-volume church, found on re-review and verified here: you cannot walk from the nave into the crossing.**

`_find_perimeters` gives every building id its own CLOSED ring and `_place_doors` puts openings only where a part meets open ground. Measured on the cruciform plan: 8 nave cells abut the crossing and NOT ONE of them carries a door. The five volumes get 9 doors between them and every one is external. So the plan is five sealed rooms you enter separately from outdoors -- and the cruciform has no west door at all, both nave doors being mid-flank.

This is `church-volumes-break-four-passes` arriving as a playability failure rather than a tidiness one. It is not enough to stop doubling the wall; something has to express **an opening BETWEEN two ids**, which nothing in the codebase does today. A chancel arch, a crossing arch and a transept arch are all that shape.

Blocks everything: no plan can be pasted for real use until it is walkable, and no interior or scene built on one means anything. Do this before any further plan work.

DONE 2026-09-01, by omission rather than by a door. _find_perimeters now treats siblings of one complex as the same building, so the shared wall is never recorded and never built -- that IS the chancel arch. The parts keep their own ids for the two things that should differ across the join, the roof and the course count. _place_doors skips a subordinate part, so a chancel has no street door: measured, 0 doors on the chancel where it previously had 2.

tasks.what: The piers break the cross-nave line; the long view was the problem
tasks.note:
The arcade was built to answer 'a 6-wide nave is a bowling alley with total sightlines'. Re-review says it does not, and reading `_arcade` back, it is right: the piers run in two COLUMNS ALONG the long axis, so they break the cross-nave line -- which was never the complaint -- and leave the axial line untouched.

Measured: aisled and minster naves span x4-12 with piers at x5 and x11, so the central span is **5 cells / 25 ft clear for the full 90 ft**. The hall church is worse at 6 cells / 30 ft clear over 80 ft, which is exactly the width round one condemned, and shortbow normal range to the foot. Round one's bowling alley lost one cell of width and gained two side lanes.

The lanes are worth having -- five piers in line genuinely break line of effect along an aisle -- but they are **1 cell wide, so no Large creature fits**, and the piers are full height so nothing shoots over them.

The fix is CROSS-AXIS, and the review names it: a **rood screen** across the chancel arch with one opening. It cuts the 90 ft lane the arcade missed, makes the chancel a defensible second room, and -- the reason to do this one first -- it is a partial wall WITH AN OPENING, so building it forces exactly the shared-boundary machinery `church-parts-have-no-way-between-them` needs anyway.

Also: `_arcade` only builds on `role == 'nave'`, so the cruciform's 8x8 crossing has ZERO piers and is the largest unobstructed room on the board, with the tower standing on nothing. Four piers inset one cell would make it the ambush node it is supposed to be.

tasks.what: The corrections added 50% area and pushed the board past a fight
tasks.note:
Widening the naves cost more than it looks. The aisled nave went 108 -> 162 cells, about +50%, for one cell of usable lane each side. The cruciform is now **26x39 tiles = 130x195 ft, about 47 cells corner to corner** -- 8 moves at 30 ft, 4 dashing -- so half the board is outside any three-round fight.

And a 9-10 cell nave means a five-character party **cannot form a line**: it takes 9 bodies to hold the width, and the new aisles route past whatever they do hold.

So width is not free and the sweet spot is under 9. This pulls against `church-section-is-too-tall-for-its-width`, which wants width to justify the height already shipped -- the two want deciding together rather than one at a time.

Note the ranking did not move between rounds (cruciform > minster > narthex > aisled) and the reviewer calls that the finding: the corrections were applied uniformly, so they moved all four by the same amount and settled nothing about which plan to keep.

tasks.what: Wire church_parts and lay_spire into the town build, and report it
tasks.note:
**VERIFIED 2026-09-01, and it is the worst finding of the day.** The only writer of tm.church_parts is tools/church_plans.py, and the only caller of lay_spire is the same file. On a real import tm.church_parts is empty.

So SUBORDINATE_STEP reaches **zero** buildings, church_courses falls through to its single-building branch on every temple in every town, and **no board gets a spire**. Both were written up in the same session as corrections that had landed.

This is the 1,084 stacks failure again -- at 0% instead of 2% -- in a repo whose CLAUDE.md carries that lesson under its own heading. The check that exists for exactly this, verify.feature_report, built after fences shipped absent from every board reviewed, **does not know about church parts or spires**, so nothing said a word.

Two halves, and the report half is what stops the next recurrence:
1. Split a temple polygon into roles in the raster, and call lay_spire from _lay_towers.
2. Add both to feature_report on the FAILING branch: a temple offered and not split, or a tower built with no spire, is a FAIL and not an 'ok, none here'. A town does not decline to have churches in it.

Recommended first version, sized to real data rather than to the plans: **one nave plus one chancel**, 9x7 + 4x4 = 79 cells, inside the imported range, exercising SUBORDINATE_STEP for its single step. Explicitly do NOT author a fifth plan or tune the step table -- tuning a table nothing reads is the loop this round is already in.

DONE 2026-09-01. split_churches runs in rasterize; _lay_towers calls lay_spire on the tower block. verify.feature_report has a churches branch on the FAILING side: a temple over the split threshold that came out one box is a FAIL, and a tower with no spire is a FAIL. Forest Church now reports '1 church(es); 1 split into nave and chancel; 1 with a tower, 1 spire(s)'.

**It caught a real bug within minutes of existing.** TileMap.crop builds a fresh map and copies field by field, and it did not copy church_parts -- so every crop rebuilt the church as one box with the chancel sealed and its own street door. The line read 'BIG ENOUGH TO SPLIT AND NOT SPLIT' on a church that had been split perfectly well. That is the check doing exactly the job it was written for, on its first day.

tasks.what: church_parts finds the FIRST nave on the map, not this church's
tasks.note:
church_courses takes the first nave in the WHOLE MAP. With two churches in one town, every part of the second bands against the first's nave: a 30-cell chapel's chancel beside a 102-cell church gets four courses on a two-course nave -- a chancel twice the height of the church it belongs to. The roof reads the same function so it will not float; it will just be wrong, silently, which is worse.

East Tradebourne has FOUR temples, so this is not hypothetical.

Fix: map each part to (nave_bid, role), with a nave mapping to itself. O(1), unambiguous, and it survives a second church.

Two more on the same function. **Its docstring contradicts its code**: it says it reads the footprint off the TileMap because footprints() exists precisely so three passes cannot disagree -- then does a raw full WxD scan, twice per call, from storeys_of, which the shell, the floors and the roof all call per cell. On East Tradebourne that is 441k cells per lookup. Use footprints(tm).

And re-import renumbering is not a hazard today because the TileMap is rebuilt per build -- but it becomes one the moment splitting moves to IMPORT time, where it has to go, because roles then persist in layout.json beside floors. Design the key for that now rather than twice.

tasks.what: lay_spire can hover a cap over a gap, and takes an unnamed height
tasks.note:
The fixed 4x4 cap is defensible; the unchecked PLACEMENT is not.

xs and zs in lay_spire are sorted DISTINCT coordinates, not a contiguous range, and the four pieces go down without ever testing membership in cells. A ring-shaped or split tower footprint therefore puts the cap in the gap between the parts, hovering over the nave -- and _lay_towers' by_building merges all of a building's tower cells into ONE set, so a west-front pair of towers is exactly that case. Guard: require the chosen 4x4 to be a subset of cells, and group tower cells by connected component rather than by building id.

Second: lay_spire takes a bare y float and never says whether it is a base or a top, and church_plans.py passes max(p.y for p in b.placements) -- the ORIGIN of the tallest placement anywhere on the map, not the top of anything. That is how a floating spire ships. Name the argument and derive it inside.

DONE 2026-09-01. The argument is named base_y and lay_spire refuses a cap that is not wholly inside the tower block (xs/zs are distinct coordinates, not a contiguous range, and _lay_towers merges a building's tower cells into one set -- so a west-front pair would have put the cap in the gap between them). Verified on the built slab before pasting: the spire's feet sit at y=19.5 and 20 castle wall pieces top out at exactly 19.5. Seated, measured, not eyeballed.

tasks.what: Five of the plan guards restate the literal they check
tasks.note:
I wrote 22 tests to guard the plans after shipping a plan whose caption lied about its geometry. Re-review says five cannot catch a regression, and reading them back it is right -- **nothing in the file calls build()**, so _arcade and _tilemap are untested by construction.

- test_the_arcade_leaves_an_aisle_on_each_side asserts PIER_SPACING >= 2: a constant against a constant, under a geometric name. _arcade returning 0 on a palette miss passes it.
- test_every_church_plan_builds_what_its_name_says -- check()'s aisle clause also only reads PIER_SPACING, and the rest compares a string literal to a tuple literal in the same dict. It cannot see any geometry.
- test_every_plan_terminates_in_a_chancel asserts PRESENCE, never position: a chancel at the west end passes.
- test_every_plan_has_exactly_one_nave and test_no_nave_is_a_corridor restate the literal.

The five that do work call real code: the two subordinate_courses tests, the crawlspace floor, the transept/crossing adjacency computation, and the height-spread test.

**And one of them is actively harmful.** test_no_nave_is_a_corridor asserts nave_width >= 8. An 8-wide nave four deep is 32 cells, so the suite has encoded the impossibility of fitting the MEDIAN REAL CHURCH at 65 cells. A guard written against a play complaint is now a guard against real data.

tasks.what: No church plan has a tower, because the width fix removed it
tasks.note:
**VERIFIED. pick_towers returns ZERO cells for the aisled, cruciform and hall plans, and the minster's 25 tower cells are on temple-0004 -- the cloister RANGE. Ninety feet of tower over the dormitory and nothing over the church.**

TOWER_MIN_ASPECT is 2.5 and it is a nave-SHAPE test. Measured: round one's 6x18 nave is aspect 3.00 and got 36 tower cells; round two's 9x18 is aspect 2.00 and gets none. The cruciform's 8x15 is 1.88. **The corridors had towers; the corrected naves do not.** So the fix for 'the tower is the full width of the nave' was to widen the nave, and widening the nave removed the tower altogether -- which is also why the same rule handed the minster's tower to a 5x15 range at aspect 3.0.

This is the same inversion tower-compact-plan already records from the other side: the aspect gate reads compactness as 'not a nave', and a compact plan at 90+ cells is a nave WITH AISLES, which is precisely the church that has a tower. Two independent findings now point at one gate.

**And TOWER_INSET does not exist.** It is cited in tools/church_plans.py's own module docstring as the thing holding the tower a cell off each flank. Nothing in the codebase defines it. I wrote about a constant I never implemented, in the same file where I added a check against captions lying about geometry.

So both plan captions that mention a tower are false about their own geometry, again, one round after that exact failure was supposed to have been guarded.

tasks.what: Add lean-to aisles under their own roofs; stop widening the nave
tasks.note:
The width correction went too far and in the wrong form. 9 cells by 5 courses is 45 x 50 ft -- a nave you could roll on its side; the hall plan at 10 wide is a square section. Salisbury's nave is 34 x 84 ft, about 2.5:1, and a good parish arcade is 18-20 ft wide by 30-35 to the wallplate.

**The mistake was widening the VESSEL instead of adding AISLES.** Piers one cell in give a 5 ft passage with no lean-to roof over it and no clerestory above, so all four plans are still single volumes IN SECTION -- which is the thing an aisled church is defined by. Keep the arcade span at 6-7 cells and hang 2-cell aisles under their own lower roofs; that is Lavenham, and unlike a wider box it reads from outside.

It also un-breaks widening-the-nave-deleted-the-tower: a 6-7 cell vessel keeps the aspect that earns a tower, and the aisles are separate volumes that do not enter the aspect test.

The 40 ft chancel against a 50 ft nave is right and should stay.

Related and worth doing together: A's east end now has chapel and vestry flanking the chancel, which gives three parallel roofs at 30/40/30 and BURIES the chancel gable and its east window. Vestry to the north only; the chapel belongs off the nave's east bay.

tasks.what: building_ranges re-splits each part after SUBORDINATE_STEP
tasks.note:
The part tables state one course count per volume and it is false for about 39% of every nave. building_ranges runs AFTER SUBORDINATE_STEP and splits a large footprint into two ranges at different heights, so every part is re-split behind the banding: aisled and minster naves come out 99 cells at 5 courses and 63 at 4; the hall church 100/60; the cruciform's nave 72/48 and its **crossing 40/24**.

The crossing is the one volume that must not step -- three equal gables meeting is the whole reason SUBORDINATE_STEP gives a transept the nave's own height -- and it steps.

The mid-nave ridge step is NOT new; a 6x18 nave splits 66/42 too. What is new is that the tables and the task notes now assert a single figure that the geometry does not carry. Either building_ranges skips a part with a church role, or the tables have to report both.

tasks.what: The spire is a fleche mid-nave, not a cap on a tower
tasks.note:
All four spires are four pieces on a 4x4 centred on the NAVE. On the cruciform it lands at z10-13 while the crossing is z19-26: a fleche squatting on a nave ridge, seven cells from the tower it was meant to cap. church_plans.py picks the nave because it is the first part, and lay_spire has no opinion about what it is capping.

Downstream of widening-the-nave-deleted-the-tower: there is no tower to put it on. Fix that first, then call lay_spire from _lay_towers on the tower block rather than from the plan tool on whatever is biggest.

Proportion, separately: the fixed 4x4 cap is 40-44% of the nave's width and 20 ft tall on a 20 ft base -- a 45-degree cap. Ketton's broach is nearer 3:1. Once it stands on a tower rather than a nave the base is right, but the rise probably wants stacking rather than one course.

DONE 2026-09-01, in two steps. `lay_spire` is called from `_lay_towers` on the tower block (church-work-reaches-zero-real-buildings), and the design pass squared that block so the cap fills it: overhead on `ET tower 09-01` the spire is the whole tower top, finial centred, inside the parapet. The proportion complaint moved to `church-spire-proportion`.

tasks.what: Square set-back tower, one-kit top, belfry stage
tasks.note:
From the user's close-up of a 09-01e board: red terracotta scraps wedged between the spire and the parapet, and a tower elevation reading as an office block. Measured before designing: the tower was an **8x4 full-width end strip** -- the carve took every cell within `side` of the end while its own comment claimed a set-back (`TOWER_INSET` all over again, geometry behind the prose). The 4x4 spire covered half of it and `_lay_towers` hipped the rest in the building's dealt ROOF_MIX kit: 8 Village slopes and 4 corners of red house-roof on a stone church tower.

Three changes, each pinned by a test that reads the built slab:
1. **Square, centred carve** (`test_a_church_tower_is_square`): side x side, so nave wall and roof show past the tower on both flanks -- the set-back finally exists. All five towers across the towns now 4x4.
2. **One-kit top** (`test_a_church_tower_top_is_one_kit`): on a one-volume building the margin cells pave as wall-walk stone and the roof-mix hip never runs; census on temple-0027's crop went from '20 crenellation + 8 Village slope + 4 Village corner + 4 spire' to '12 crenellation + 4 spire'.
3. **Belfry** (`test_the_belfry_is_the_only_glazed_tower_stage`): the top stage gets one centred civic-window opening per face -- 8 pieces at one course on the crop -- and the middle stages stay blind, which breaks the band-on-band stack.

PROVEN THROUGH THE PREVIEWER, which was the point of the exercise: the before/after slabs live in `out/spiredesign/` where the Slabs screen lists them, the proof page (artifact `3940603b`) is drawn by `slab_axon`/`slab_svg` themselves, and the top census is the same data the screen's legend serves. The collider caveat held too -- the previewer proved kit and massing, and the mesh questions went to a board (`ET tower 09-01`).

Two test drafts were wrong before the geometry was: one flagged the stage FLOORS as roof-mix offenders, one predicted stage heights instead of reading them off the built walls. Both now read the data.

tasks.what: A 45-degree cap is not a broach spire; probe a taller tier
tasks.note:
The architectural review's remaining point, still true after the design pass: the 4x4 cap is 20 ft tall on a 20 ft base -- 45 degrees -- where a real broach spire (Ketton) is nearer 3:1. The fix is not a rotation or a bigger cap; it is HEIGHT, and the kit may already carry it: `Tall 1x1x4` is 1x4x2 (a half-width steep plane) and `Tall 1x1x2` exists. A second, narrower tier stacked on the 4x4 -- or the 4x4's own pieces raised on a 2-course drum of wall -- would take the silhouette from 45 to ~60 degrees.

NOT PROBED, and the spire's own history says what that means: the first spire attempt swept rotations on the wrong pieces, concluded scale, and was settled by a hand-build that used pieces nobody had tried. Probe the candidates side by side on one board (the previewer settles massing first, the board settles the meshes), and keep the current cap as the control bay.

Also noted on the side shot, minor: the tower shaft is two-tone -- the shell courses wear the building's dark dealt fabric and the added stages wear tan `castle wall 1x1`. It reads almost like intentional quoining; decide whether to keep it when the spire tier is probed, since both change the same elevation.

PROBED 2026-09-01, three boards (`PROBE spire tiers`, `tiers2`, `tiers3`), and **the two-tier spire is DEAD in this kit.**

- `Tall 1x1x4` does not close a 2x2 needle at ANY quarter turn. Swept all four offsets on one board with the known-good cap as control: every bay is a crossed X of open planes with the timber back faces showing. It is not a pyramid face piece, so the broach and spike assemblies built on it are dead too. The first sweep also mis-placed two faces on one cell -- the arithmetic said offset 0 gives the right footprints, and the board then said footprints were never the problem.
- The cross-kit pinnacle (`Palace Marble roof tower`, 1x4x1, half-cell centred and lapped into the cap) closes GEOMETRICALLY and fails on MATERIAL: the piece is teal-and-gold ornament against dark shingle. Exactly the question the previewer cannot answer and one board can.

**What the kit CAN do -- three closed silhouettes, all proven on the board:**
1. `Tall 2x2x4 Corner out` -- the shipping 45-degree pyramid (control).
2. `Tall 2x2x4 corner round` -- a CONICAL spire, witch-hat silhouette, seam ribs visible up one face.
3. `Tall 2x2x4 corner out unique` -- an ornamented, crocketed spire, the richest of the three.

So proportion beyond 1:1 is not available from the spire itself; total height is the tower's job and `CHURCH_BANDS` already scales its stages. The live question is a TASTE one: keep the pyramid everywhere, or deal the conical/ornamented caps for variety -- e.g. the crocketed one on `great`-band churches. Left for the owner; the decision board is `PROBE spire tiers3` and `tools/spire_probe.py` rebuilds the sweep.

**LARGE SPIRE PROBED 2026-09-01 (`PROBE spire large`, `tools/spire_large_probe.py`), and it CLOSES.** The arithmetic that motivated it: `Tall 2x2x4` rises 4 over 2 deep, so a ring stepping in 2 and up 4 keeps one continuous ~63-degree plane. An 8x8 -- one ring of edge and corner pieces ending on the proven 4x4 cap -- swept over all four edge offsets with the cap as control:

- **edge +6 closes**, verified from BOTH sides of the board; 0, 12 and 18 show open faces and inward slopes. That is exactly `ROOF_ROT_OFFSET_WIDE['castle fortified']` = (6, 0): the tall family follows the kit's wide-family table, edges +6 and corners +0.
- The result is **8 tiles (40 ft) of sealed spire on an 8x8 base**, twice the steepness of the 45-degree cap and the best-looking assembly any of these probes has produced.
- A 6x6 is impossible (its top ring is the 2x2 peak the needle sweep killed); a 12x12 should telescope by the same plane rule but is UNPROBED -- do not claim it.

**RECOMMENDATION, with the reasoning on the table:**
1. **Ship the 45-degree pyramid cap as the default**, unchanged. It fits every tower the four towns actually carve (all 4x4) and is settled by the hand-build.
2. **Do NOT wire the 8x8 large spire yet.** No church today can host it: the widest real nave is 8 cells, and an 8-wide tower needs a 9-wide nave under the set-back rule. Wiring it now creates a feature that reaches zero real buildings -- the exact failure this project hit twice in one day and built a report line against. The recipe is recorded here and in the probe tool; wire it WHEN a consumer exists, and extend the churches feature line in the same commit.
3. **The consumer to build toward is the cruciform CROSSING**, which is already 8x8 in the plan proposals -- a 40 ft crossing spire over 50 ft walls is a 90 ft silhouette and the strongest church form this kit can make. Second candidate: let great-band churches with naves >= 9 carve an 8-wide tower.
4. The conical and crocketed 4x4 caps remain the live TASTE option -- crocketed on great-band churches is my pick, dealt like the roof mix so a town is not uniform. Owner's call, decision board `PROBE spire tiers3`.

tasks.what: --check maps cloister to range and never looks at geometry
tasks.note:
The guard I added against captions lying about geometry passes two plans whose captions lie about their geometry.

- **The minster has no cloister.** One range, flush against the nave's east wall: no garth, nothing 'inset a cell', no walk. check() maps the word 'cloister' to the role 'range', finds a range, and passes.
- **The hall church's chapel still hangs off the middle of the nave** (x10-14, z8-13; its chancel is at z20-25). The 'parts flank the chancel' correction never reached plan C at all, and nothing noticed.
- Its aisle clause reads the global PIER_SPACING, so it can never fail for any plan.

check() compares string literals to tuple literals in the same dict. It cannot see _tilemap, _arcade, pick_towers or the built slab, so it cannot answer any question worth asking. It has to read GEOMETRY -- is there a ring of parts round an open court, does the chapel touch the chancel, did the arcade lay pieces, did anything get a tower.

tasks.what: Split the imported church polygon into nave and chancel
tasks.note:
REVIEWED 2026-09-01 by three independent critiques of `tools/church_plans.py` (artifact `1f6f4992`), and the plans did not survive.

**The headline, verified against the code: the four hand-authored plans are 176/178/220/267 cells against a real imported range of 30-102.** Plan A's NAVE ALONE (120) is larger than the largest church any export has produced (Forest Church, 102). They are 1.7x to 2.6x oversize -- not templates needing a trim, a different building class.

The recommendation, argued against the alternatives: **subdivide the imported polygon.** Templating requires scaling, and a template scaled to a 30-cell polygon gives an 8-cell vestry -- a shed; it also re-imposes a rectangle and throws away the one thing the export gave us, a real outline at a real angle. Growing into the yard fights machinery that already exists and already has checks (yards, `_absorb_open_country`, fence runs, the boundary-in-street test, the gate apron that already cost three wall towers to over-paving).

MEASURED here, a 75/25 nave/chancel cut on the seven real temples: 102 -> 77/25, 88 -> 66/22, 81 -> 61/20, 65 -> 49/16, 52 -> 39/13, and 30 -> 23/8 which is too small to be two rooms. So the split works on 5 of 7, and wants a measured minimum-area gate plus a REPORT LINE for the ones below it -- 'churches: 7; 5 split, 2 below the threshold'. That is the sentence the 2% chimney taught us to write.

Smallest honest ship: nave + chancel only. Two volumes, one join, derived from the polygon, chancel at parent-1 courses, no door of its own, tower picked on the nave. Paste one town and look before any four-volume plan is written.

DONE 2026-09-01. raster.split_churches, called before _find_perimeters. Derived from the imported polygon: the long axis is cut at CHANCEL_SHARE (25%) on the end FURTHEST FROM A STREET -- the altar end in practice, and measurable, where 'away from the door' would be circular because doors are placed after. Inset one cell each flank so the join reads as a step. Ids are suffixes (temple-0002+chancel), never new numbers. Measured on Forest Church: 102 cells -> nave 82 + chancel 15, the 5 lost to the inset. CHURCH_MIN_SPLIT_CELLS is 50, which leaves 2 of the 7 real temples unsplit and REPORTS them rather than lowering the bar.

tasks.what: Piers, a rood screen and a crypt -- the church has no play in it
tasks.note:
From the tabletop critique of the four plans (artifact `1f6f4992`), and it outranks every difference between them: **all four naves are empty boxes.** A 6x20 nave is 30x100 ft with total sightlines end to end. A shortbow's normal range is 16 tiles, so every ranged attacker covers the whole nave from turn one while the melee walks three turns to reach anything; a 20 ft fireball is 4 tiles and spans a 6-wide nave wall to wall, so there is no spreading out and no decision.

In value order, and none of it is decoration:
1. **Arcade piers** -- 1-cell piers one tile in from each long wall, every third tile. Splits a 6-wide nave into 1/4/1, gives cover every 15 ft, breaks the sightline. Cheapest fix, largest effect, and it is what makes a nave AISLED (see `church-aisles`).
2. **A rood screen** across the chancel arch with one opening: turns a 20-tile run into two rooms and a chokepoint.
3. **A crypt** under the chancel. No plan has one, and it is the standard reason a party is in a church at night.
4. **Tower interiors** -- a floor at course 2 and 4, a bell chamber, a ladder. The towers are solid massing today, which is also why `church-one-volume` had to keep `_lay_towers`' stage floors.
5. **A gallery** over the aisles at 10 ft with a stair: archers shooting down is what TaleSpire does better than paper.
6. **A second door** -- a priest's door into the chancel. Every plan is one-way, so there is no flank and no escape.

Ranked for play, the four plans came out **cruciform > minster > narthex > aisled**, and the reason is the crossing: four corridors meeting at one cell, with each 5x5 transept invisible from the nave until you reach it. That is the only genuinely broken sightline on the page, and the tower stands over it, putting the verticality where the fight already is.

tasks.what: Fix or drop the plan named 'aisled' that has no aisles
tasks.note:
MINE, and caught by review rather than by me. `PLANS['aisled']` in `tools/church_plans.py` is captioned 'Aisled parish church' and its parts are nave, chancel, chapel, vestry -- **there are no aisles in it**. Checked: `any('aisle' in part)` is False.

That is worse than a bad plan. A probe whose label promises something its geometry does not contain is the same failure as a count that is not a shape: a reviewer reads the caption, sees a long church, and confirms a thing that was never built. It is the `1,084 stacks` line again in a different costume.

Two honest resolutions: build the aisles (which is `church-aisles` and `church-is-an-empty-box-for-play` item 1, piers rather than separate volumes), or rename the plan to what it is -- a nave with a chancel, a chapel and a vestry. The tabletop review recommends cutting the plan outright, on the grounds that the cruciform does everything it does with a better node. A test that every plan's parts match its name would stop the next one.

DONE 2026-09-01. Naves are 8-10 cells wide now and carry an ARCADE -- piers one cell in from each long wall every three cells -- which is what makes a nave aisled, breaks the sightline the tabletop review called a bowling alley, and gives cover every 15 ft. `tools/church_plans.py --check` fails any plan whose caption promises a part its geometry does not contain, which is the guard against the next one.

tasks.what: A nave 30 ft wide should not stand 50 ft to the eaves
tasks.note:
**This is a criticism of `church-size-ladder`, which shipped the same day.** Reviewed against real churches: a parish nave is roughly as tall to the wall-plate as it is wide. Forest Church's temple is 6 cells wide = 30 ft, and the `great` band now stands it 5 courses = 50 ft to the eaves, with the ridge measured at 66 ft. That is Westminster Abbey proportion on a parish footprint.

So the ladder keyed on AREA does the right thing for the wrong reason: a 6x20 nave has a great-church *area* and a parish-church *width*, and height should follow the width. A long thin church got tall because it was long.

**The important consequence: 'make it bigger' is not 'make it taller'.** The user asked for a larger church and the ladder answered with height; the review says the section is already over-tall and what is missing is WIDTH and FORM -- aisles, transepts, a chancel, a set-back tower. Worth settling before the ladder is tuned again, because the two pull opposite ways.

Candidate key: courses from the nave's WIDTH (span), with area only deciding whether it earns a tower and aisles.

tasks.what: A tower the full width of the nave is a westwork, not a tower
tasks.note:
**Called the biggest silhouette defect in the architectural review, and it is on three of the four plans and on the real towns too.** `pick_towers` takes a square block off the end of the footprint, so the tower comes out the FULL WIDTH of the nave: 6-in-6 on the aisled and cruciform plans, 7-in-7 on the minster, and 6-in-7 on Forest Church's own temple.

The tower's own proportion is fine -- 30 ft square and 122 ft tall is Lavenham. What is wrong is that it is flush on both flanks with no set-back, so it reads as a westwork or a keep rather than a tower rising out of a roofline. This is also why the first two shots of the `church-one-volume` review looked like a stone cliff: end-on, a full-width tower IS the building.

Fix is small: inset the tower block one cell on each flank where the footprint allows, so a course of nave wall and roof shows past it on both sides. On a 6-wide nave that is a 4x4 tower, which at 20 ft square is still a real parish tower.

tasks.what: Fix where each plan's ancillary volumes attach
tasks.note:
Every one of the four plans in `tools/church_plans.py` puts at least one volume in the wrong place, read off the built geometry rather than the captions:

- **aisled**: chapel and vestry both attach to the MIDDLE of the nave, beside the tower. A vestry belongs north of the CHANCEL and a chapel flanking the chancel (Long Melford, Lavenham); mid-nave is where a porch goes and nothing else. Also has no aisles -- see `church-plan-a-has-no-aisles`.
- **cruciform**: the transepts sit mid-nave at z11-15 while the chancel begins at z22, so **the crossing is 35 ft from where the transepts are**, and the tower is on the west end rather than over it. Both claims in my caption are false in the geometry.
- **narthex**: **there is no chancel.** A hall church still terminates in a presbytery or apse (Soest, Landshut). It is a box with a lobby, and the silhouette review ranked it last -- reads as a guildhall or a tithe barn.
- **minster**: no chancel, no crossing, chapter house at the WEST end beside the tower when it belongs off the east range next to the transept (Fountains, Rievaulx), and no cloister WALKS -- the arcade round the garth is what makes a cloister legible. The garth is 25x35 ft against Salisbury's 145 ft square: a light well, not a cloister.

Cheapest fix each: aisled, change two z-offsets so chapel and vestry flank the chancel. Cruciform, slide both transepts down to abut the chancel and put the tower on the crossing. Narthex, add one chancel volume opposite the lobby. Minster, inset the ranges one cell and roof that strip low as a walk.

Silhouette ranking from the same review: **cruciform > aisled > minster > narthex**, which disagrees with the tabletop ranking only about the aisled plan.

DONE 2026-09-01. Chapel and vestry flank the CHANCEL; the cruciform's transepts abut the chancel so the crossing is a real crossing and the tower stands over it; the hall church and the minster both terminate in a chancel; the minster's ranges are inset so the cloister walk reads. Heights follow `SUBORDINATE_STEP` so the three gables at a crossing are equal.

tasks.what: A multi-volume church needs a parent map before it can ship
tasks.note:
'A church complex is several abutting building ids' is sound for MASSING and a hack for everything else. Both verified on the built plan rather than argued:

- **`_place_doors` is the worst.** It gives every bid a doorway to the most public space it touches. Measured on plan A: **7 doors across 4 volumes for one church** -- the vestry gets its own street door and the chancel gets two exterior doors where an arch belongs. Nothing in the codebase expresses 'opening between two ids'.
- **Walls double at every join.** Each bid closes its own perimeter: 104 perimeter cells across the four volumes, so the nave's interior shows the chancel's OUTSIDE, and `tile_interpenetration` jumps off its 557 baseline.
- **Roofs**: per-bid hips are right, but a lower roof meeting a taller wall has no valley and buries into it.
- **Chunking**: 'a building's shell is never split across chunks' becomes per-volume rather than per-church, and `--per-building` writes four slabs for one church.
- **Scenes**: one board per bid, so a church becomes four boards, and `hall_layout` BSPs a 24-cell chancel as if it were a building.
- **verify** counts four enterable buildings where there is one church.

A parent map (`tm.parent[bid]`) is the shape of the fix: doors, verify counts and scene codes see one entity while the geometry stays per-volume. **Ids must be suffixes** (`temple-0002.chancel`), never new numbers -- both importers number from one global counter and `boards.json` MOVED detection keys on it, so minting ids would renumber the town.

tasks.what: Band a subordinate volume against its nave, not by its own area
tasks.note:
`church_band` bands by AREA, and on a multi-volume church that breaks two ways.

1. A 24-cell chancel lands in `chapel` -- 2 courses, 20 ft -- against a 5-course 50 ft nave. That is a 40% step. A real chancel is 70-85% of the nave.
2. **The discreteness leaks into relationships.** In the minster plan the south range (40 cells) gets 3 courses and the chapter house (36) gets 2: four cells of difference draws a 10 ft step between two ranges of one cloister, an accident of where a band boundary fell, visible from across the board.

Fix: `church_band` decides the PRINCIPAL volume only; subordinates are `parent - 1` (chancel, transept, range) or `parent - 2` (porch, vestry), clamped at 2. The step becomes a function of ROLE, which is what says church, rather than of a cell count crossing a rung.

Note for whoever does it: `pick_towers` reads per-bid width/depth against `TOWER_MIN_ASPECT`, so after subdivision a shortened nave can LOSE the tower it qualified for as one box, and a 5x5 transept can qualify for its own. The tower has to be picked for the complex, once.

**Two independent reviews converged on this, and the architectural one gives the numbers.** A chancel is SMALL IN PLAN AND TALL IN SECTION, because it is the most important space in the building -- so keying height on footprint area gets it exactly backwards. 30 ft is about double the right step: nave 5 courses -> chancel **4** (a 10 ft step), with chapel, vestry, porch and aisle at 2.

**Transepts must be 5, not 2.** Three equal gables meeting is what makes a cruciform church read as cruciform; at 20 ft the arms are lean-tos that disappear from every view but overhead. So `parent - 1` is not a blanket rule either -- a transept is `parent`, a chancel `parent - 1`, and the minor rooms a floor of 2.

DONE 2026-09-01. `build.SUBORDINATE_STEP` + `subordinate_courses`, with the role carried on `raster.TileMap.church_parts` -- beside `floors` and for the same reason, that the shell, the upper floors and the roof all read it and a roof that disagrees with the walls floats. Measured on the revised plans: nave 50 ft, transept 50, chancel 40, chapel/vestry/narthex/range 30. A floor of 2 courses stops any step reaching a crawlspace.

tasks.what: Decide whether a church may grow beyond the polygon it was given
tasks.note:
The height ladder is done and the footprint is not, because the footprint is NOT OURS: it comes from the MFCG/FTG export as a polygon, and the largest temple in five towns is 102 cells (6x19 = 30x95 ft). `docs/great-buildings.md` §1.3 calls 12-18 x 5-7 cells a large town church, so the imported ones are in band -- there is no cathedral in any export because the generators do not draw one.

So 'a bigger church' past this point means one of three things, and which one is a DESIGN CALL rather than a measurement:
  1. Grow the polygon into its own yard, which is the only free ground. Cheap, bounded, and worth about 20-30 percent.
  2. Annex a neighbouring plot, which means deleting a building the export authored. That is the first place citysmith would overrule its source, and the precedent matters more than the church does.
  3. Leave the footprint and buy apparent size with HEIGHT and FORM -- spire (`church-spire`), aisles and a clerestory (`church-aisles`), a chancel step (`church-nave-and-chancel`). None of these touches the polygon.

Route 3 is the recommendation on the evidence: the ladder alone took Forest Church's temple from 6 courses to 11 with no footprint change at all, and the three form tasks are already filed and already designed.

tasks.what: Let a compact aisled church have a tower
tasks.note:
pick_towers gates on TOWER_MIN_ASPECT 2.5, so East Tradebourne's two largest temples (88 cells at 8x12, aspect 1.50; 81 cells at 10x9, aspect 1.11) are towerless while a 65-cell one is the landmark. A compact plan at 88 cells is a nave WITH aisles, which is the church that has a tower -- the gate is inverted with respect to its own docstring.

DONE 2026-09-01. TOWER_ASPECT_EXEMPT_TILES waives the aspect gate above 75 cells. Arrived at from three directions: East Tradebourne's two LARGEST temples were towerless while a 65-cell one was the landmark; widening the plan naves took 6x18 from aspect 3.00 to 2.00 and deleted the tower from three plans while handing the minster's to a cloister range; and splitting a chancel off Forest Church took its nave from 3.17 to 2.33 and deleted that one too. Every improvement to a church shortens its nave, and the gate punished exactly that. 75 clears 81, 82 and 88 and still refuses a house.

tasks.what: Let a caller ask walls.families for a course height other than 2.0
tasks.note: _prune_to_one_course returns all 22 families at 2.0, which is right for a house and hides Moorgoth LargeWall 01/02 (1 x 4.0 x 2 and 1 x 4.0 x 1) from every caller. A 4.0 wall is a 20 ft eaves in one course, which is exactly what the barn and the hall want. Loosening the pruning is the wrong fix; asking for a height is the right one.

tasks.what: Stand a market cross at the centre of the square
tasks.note:
NO CANDIDATE PIECE EXISTS and none has been probed. Nearest by shape: Castle Ruins Pillar Base/Mid/Top, Moorgoth Buttress Spire, Palace Marble pillar base/mid. Shortlist by render with tools/asset_shots.py, then probe -- a render shortlists and a probe decides.

DONE 2026-09-01, **settled by a slab the user built by hand** (`tests/fixtures/handbuilt_turret.slab`) -- the fourth hand-build to beat a probe, and the second to correct a misuse of a quarter piece.

`Palace Marble roof tower` (1x4x1) is not a pinnacle: it is a QUARTER of a two-stage domed turret -- arcaded body, teal dome, gold ornament -- and four of them on a 2x2 at `ROOF_CORNER_ROT` + 0 close it. That is the third hand-build in a row whose rotations are exactly the corner table: the spire cap, the verge, now this. My spire probe had placed the same piece WHOLE, half-cell centred, and called it a material clash; the actual failure was using a quarter as a unit, `md_tower_wall_01` all over again.

Wired: `palette` pins the piece under `market_cross` (OPTIONAL_ROLES, degrades to nothing), deliberately cross-pack -- Marble Palace on a medieval board is the owner's explicit call ('any style is fine'), and the medieval pack has no candidate at all. `_lay_market_cross` assembles the quadrants; `_dress_market` gives the CENTRE of the biggest square to the cross, per docs/great-buildings.md, and the well's centroid walk then lands it a ring further out. Keep-clear ring around the cross so the stall rows stand off.

Measured on the Forest Church market crop: 4 pieces at the exact hand-build rotations, centred, seated on the plaza. Pinned by `test_the_market_cross_matches_the_slab_the_user_built`.

tasks.what: Build the rooftop terrace on a building's lower range

It was built to break up a big building's silhouette, and it produces without meaning to EXACTLY the geometry a roof terrace needs: a lower roof with a taller wall along one side of it, which is a wall the terrace door goes in. Class A = two ranges, lower >= 6 cells, >= 2 cells of shared boundary. Measured: Pelvesthollow 1 of 35 (2.9%), Graybank 4 of 150 (2.7%), East Tradebourne 95 of 989 (9.6%) -- median deck 21 cells (525 sq ft) behind a 7-cell wall. The scaling is honest by construction: a village of cottages gets one, a city gets ninety-five, with nothing tuned. THE ONE COLLISION IS MEASURED AND RESOLVES THE RIGHT WAY: all 95 candidates carry a ridge stack on the very cell the deck would occupy, because the lower range is its own roof block -- so a terraced range moves its stack to the taller range's flank, which is where a real lateral stack goes anyway. Needs chimney-forms. Also inverts one rule deliberately: `_lay_upper_floors` decks interior cells only, and a terrace MUST deck to its perimeter or there is nothing to stand on at the edge. A/B on all three towns; the two small ones should come out near-identical, the same shape gable-ends used.

tasks.what: Report the market as offered-vs-built, with the count on the square
tasks.note:
MEASURED 2026-09-01 on a 26x21 crop of Forest Church's square: the build report carries lines for chimneys, gabled ends, field walls, yards, marsh, quarters and surfaces, and **not one line about the market** -- on a crop that is 130 plaza cells. What actually stands on them is three stalls and a well.

This is the fence failure exactly: a feature correct, absent and unreported at once. It is also the chimney failure, which is the sharper one -- a COUNT is not a SHAPE. `1,084 stacks` read as success until the line said `1,084 of 1 course`. `4 market props` reads as a market until the line says `4 items on 130 plaza cells`.

A plaza does not decline to have a market on it, so the branch is the failing kind: offered (plaza cells exist) and not built (nothing stands on them) is a FAIL, not an `ok, none here`. A town with no plaza at all is the `not offered` branch and says so.

tasks.what: Stop a 6x4 wing coming out as a flat-topped box
tasks.note: BUILT. `roof_top_is_supported` decides whether a top-ring cell caps, and the ring index no longer does. Two slopes on the same ring falling opposite ways lean on each other and make a proper ridge; a corner leans on its diagonal. So the test is the NEIGHBOUR, not the ring. The defect is exactly the even/odd split: `_roof_rings` steps one cell in per course, so a wing whose short side is EVEN stops with a band two cells wide and capping all of it lost a whole course -- a 6x4 came out a flat-topped box with a 4x2 plateau. Odd short sides already pinched to a one-cell ridge line and are untouched, which two tests state separately. A/B on all three towns: **placement count IDENTICAL** in every one -- same cells, flat caps become slopes and corners. The role does NOT need repinning. `market_stall` is already a structured group query on the stall group -- pinned by kit, which is what `docs/regenerating-boards.md` Phase 1 asked for. The kit is fine; it collapses to one mesh at the deal. Probed candidates, all plausible as a market stall: Stall Empty 02 (2.01x0.76x1.01, a bare counter), Stall Magic (2.01x1.05x1.12), Stall Weapons (2.01x0.92x1.10, spears and a round shield). The control, `castle merlon 1x1`, read wrong as designed.

Why it is not a one-liner: all three are 2.01 wide so the pitch is unaffected, but the DEPTHS differ (1.01 to 1.12) and the keep-clear reservation is what `verify.market_square_open` guards -- that check exists because a stall box wider than its pitch sealed 8 cells of Forest Church's square against its own frontage. `covered(stall, mx, mz, rot)` is already computed per placement, so dealing per pitch should be safe, but it wants the market tests run and a fresh look at one square. || FIXED. `MARKET_STALL_VARIANTS` variants are resolved and deduped; the period takes the DEEPEST candidate and the pitch the WIDEST, because both are settled before a stall is dealt and so have to hold for any of them; the pick then happens per pitch with its own rotation and cross. Forest Church goes from 7 copies of one mesh to 4 Stall Magic, 2 Stall Weapons and 1 Stall Empty 02. The test was run against the UNFIXED build and does fail there, which is the only thing that makes it evidence.

SHIPPED 2026-08-31, wired into `_lay_gabled_wing` and not into `gable_infill` -- the two close different holes and both are now present, which the hand-build itself shows (it carries a `Rural Wall 01` tympanum AND two verge pieces). How far it generalises is read off the collider: the piece closes `size_y / rise` courses and is that many cells across, and where those disagree it is REFUSED and the verge stays flush -- the same 'a gable it cannot close is worse than a hip' rule the endmix path follows. MEASURED after the change, and it is the 'correct and absent' trap again: East Tradebourne lays 2,284 verge pieces against 13,120 thatch slopes, while Pelvesthollow and Graybank lay ZERO. That is right and not a defect -- both have no quarters, so `_wing_gable` hips every wing and neither town has a gabled end for a verge to close. Counting only the small towns would have read as a dead feature.

ON A BOARD 2026-09-01, and this is the verification the task had never had. `out/vergeview.slab.txt` builds two 9x5 wings side by side through the SHIPPED `_lay_gabled_wing` -- west without the verge, east with it, numbering bars of 1 and 2 cells on the ground -- and pastes as 291 placements. **A town chunk CANNOT be used for this, and that cost most of a session.** Every chunk carries the whole MAP's registration box, so it anchors on the map's centre and its own content lands up to a hundred tiles from the cursor; `Ctrl`+scroll caps at a ~40-tile frame, so the geometry is never in shot and the paste reads as having silently failed. tasks.what: Let a wall taller than its course sink into the floor without failing
tasks.note:
MEASURED on the Forest Church regen 2026-08-31: `[FAIL] shell footing: 27 building(s) do not stand on their own floor`, every one of them at y=0.47 over a floor top of 0.5, and every one the same piece -- `Tavern Wall 01`.

**The piece is 2.0 x 2.03 x 0.5.** Every other wall in the medieval set is exactly 2.00 tall. The shell seats a wall so its HEAD lands on the course line (0.5 grade + 2.0 storey = 2.5), which puts a 2.03 panel's base at 0.47. That is the arithmetic working, not failing: CLAUDE.md's rule is that the storey IS the wall and the roof seats at `floors * storey_h`, so the head is the end that has to be right. The 0.03 is absorbed at the base where the floor hides it; absorbed at the head it would leave the wall standing proud of its own eaves, which is the visible end.

So the seating is right and the CHECK has no tolerance -- `abs(y - want) > 1e-6`, exact equality, in `verify` (the message is raised at pipeline.py:415). It exists to catch two pastes disagreeing about height, which is a WHOLE COURSE error, and it is firing on 1.8 inches.

Not fixed in passing because it is a FAIL-level check and the tolerance has to be stated as a rule rather than a fudge: a shell may be sunk into its floor by the amount its panel exceeds the nominal course, and may never float above it. Wants a test per branch -- sunk-and-allowed, floating-and-failed, whole-course-and-failed -- and a look at one Tavern-fabric building on a board to confirm the base really is hidden.

SHIPPED 2026-08-31. The allowance is the panel's own excess over a whole course (`asset.size_y - round(asset.size_y)`) and nothing more, and it is ONE-SIDED: sunk by up to that is fine, floating by any amount is not. Forest Church's shell-footing FAIL is gone, and the 27 buildings were all the 2.03 panel. The test covers four branches -- sunk-and-allowed, a plain 2.0 panel held to exact equality, floating-and-failed, whole-course-and-failed.

tasks.what: Stop a plot three cells across being massed as a house
tasks.note:
MEASURED 2026-08-31 over both towns' current layouts. East Tradebourne: **80 of 989 buildings (8%) have a short side of 3 cells or less**, and the commonest shape is 3x7 -- 15 ft by 35 ft. Pelvesthollow has NONE, so this is a dense-town problem and not a general one: it is what an FTG export's terraced plots rasterise to.

Reported off a board as \"the footprint of this house is strangely thin and small\". At 15 ft across, the interior is one cell wide once both walls are taken, which is a corridor. `docs/building-massing.md` already anchors the scale on a 35 ft median frontage precisely so a party can stand inside; 15 ft is half of that and nothing checks it.

Three routes, none chosen: merge a thin plot into its neighbour so a terrace becomes one range with a party wall (which is what a real terrace IS); mass it as an outbuilding -- a lean-to or a store with no interior claim; or widen the raster's footprint where the plot has room, which is the least honest since the export drew that line. Decide against a board, not from the count: 8% of a town is a lot of buildings to change silently.

SHIPPED 2026-09-01, and the diagnosis above is WRONG. The merge route was chosen and then measured, and both of its premises failed. First: **not one thin plot touches a neighbour.** All 160 long faces of the 80 buildings are open ground, with the nearest building 2 to 8 cells away, so there is no terrace in the raster to merge. Second, and this is the real find: **all 80 came from a polygon that was not thin.** `house-0562` rasterises to an 11x10 blob of 38 cells and the best axis-aligned rectangle inside it is 3x4 -- 68% of the building thrown away. FTG exports buildings at arbitrary angles, the raster is axis-aligned, and a diagonal band has no fat rectangle in it. The thin plots are `_regularise_buildings` slicing rotated buildings, not terraced plots rasterising.

So the fix is at the source: `raster._grow_rect` widens a sliver back out, taking the polygon's own ground and free ground inside the polygon's own bounding box -- never a road, never a neighbour, never anything beyond the footprint the export drew. East Tradebourne: thin plots 79 -> 6, floor area +476 tiles (+1.4%), building count and median footprint unchanged. Graybank 2 -> 0, Forest Church 10 -> 6, Pelvesthollow had none. The 6 that remain are boxed in by roads and neighbours with nothing free to grow into, which is the honest answer rather than a forced one.

**The gate matters as much as the growth.** Widening every inscribed rectangle out to its polygon's box -- which is what the first cut did -- took East Tradebourne from 33,702 floor tiles to 60,845 and the median footprint from 30 to 54. That is a town-wide re-massing wearing a bug fix's clothes. Only a plot that is actually thin is widened, and only until it is not; `test_widening_leaves_a_plot_that_was_never_thin_alone` holds the line.

**A merge pass was built, measured and DELETED.** It merged across the eroded gap with the union checked to be a rectangle and a budget on invented ground, and with all that it fired on **1 building of 989** across four towns. Two hundred lines that fire once is the 'correct and absent' failure this repo already records twice, so it is not shipped. One measurement from it is worth keeping: read from a FINISHED TileMap the gaps between thin plots are 85-90% LANE, and read at the merge point they are 95% GROUND -- because `_trace_lanes` runs later and invents a lane in whatever open ground it finds between buildings. Taking the finished reading at face value says 'merging would pave the town's circulation', which is the opposite of the truth.

tasks.what: Dress a trade's street frontage from outdoor goods, as the yard now is
tasks.note:
**The same defect `YARD_PROPS` just fixed, still live one table down.** `TRADE_CLUTTER` (build.py:7781) maps a trade kind to a ROOM category and resolves it through `Palette.prop`, which is the interior furnisher's API -- exactly what `YARD_CLUTTER` did before 12.1. Its `stable` entry is literally `\"house\"`, so a stable's street frontage is dressed from the bedroom set.

Reported off a board as \"fireplaces should never be outside, unless this is a blacksmith\". Measured on a 90x90 crop of East Tradebourne: 25 `Forge` and 29 `Anvil` standing outdoors, and the nearest building within three cells is a SMITHY for exactly one of each. Three forges and two anvils stand beside a HOUSE; the rest have no building within three cells at all. A forge outside a smithy is right and is the one case the report allows; a forge outside a house is the bug.

The fix has a worked example to copy: `YARD_PROPS` names outdoor palette roles (`yard_smithy`, `yard_trade`, `yard_clutter`) and `_dress_yards` deals from them. `TRADE_PROPS` should do the same for the frontage, and the roles mostly exist already. Worth checking at the same time whether a forge belongs on a frontage at all rather than in the yard behind. || CORRECTION, and it matters because this note argued from it: the "three forges and two anvils beside a HOUSE" above was an artifact of measuring by NEAREST BUILDING within three cells. Re-measured by the OWNING building -- `_stack_trade_goods` sets `b.group = bid`, so every frontage prop is attributed exactly -- all 25 forges and 29 of 32 anvils belong to smithies, which is a smith working at his fire and is the case the report allows. In a dense town a smithy's own frontage prop simply sits closer to a neighbour than to its owner. What a forge beside a timber-framed wall really shows is that nothing outside a building says which trade it is, which is a different question. || FIXED. `TRADE_PROPS` names outdoor palette roles and `_stack_trade_goods` deals from them, the shape `YARD_PROPS` took. `Forge` is pinned into `yard_smithy` on purpose so the smith keeps his fire. The real leak was small and is gone: 4 interior props on that crop -- two stools and a table with chairs at a tavern, an alchemy shelf at a shop -- becomes 0, and the latent stable-to-house mapping goes with it. The frontage now also keeps off the door APRON, not merely the door cell. Two tests hold it: the table names roles and not room categories, and no yard or frontage role except `yard_smithy` may offer a hearth.
